chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 1 — Rome. A street
paragraphs: [A company of mutinous Citizens enters, carrying staves, clubs, and other weapons.]
FIRST CITIZEN. Before we go any further, listen to me.
ALL. Speak, speak!
FIRST CITIZEN. You're all determined to die rather than starve?
ALL. Determined, determined!
FIRST CITIZEN. First, you know Caius Martius is the people's worst enemy.
ALL. We know it, we know it!
FIRST CITIZEN. Let's kill him, and we'll have corn at our own price. Is that agreed?
ALL. No more talking about it; let it be done. Away, away!
SECOND CITIZEN. One word, good citizens.

FIRST CITIZEN. We're counted as poor citizens, the patricians as good. What the authorities gorge themselves on would relieve us. If they'd just give us the surplus while it's still wholesome, we might think they were treating us decently. But they think we cost too much. The thinness that afflicts us, the spectacle of our misery, is like an inventory itemizing their abundance; our suffering is their profit. Let's avenge this with our pikes before we waste away to rakes; for the gods know I say this hungry for bread, not thirsty for revenge.
SECOND CITIZEN. Would you go after Caius Martius in particular?
FIRST CITIZEN. Him first. He's an absolute dog to the common people.
SECOND CITIZEN. Do you consider what services he's done for his country?
FIRST CITIZEN. Very well, and I'd be content to give him credit for them, except that he pays himself in pride.
SECOND CITIZEN. Now, don't speak maliciously.

FIRST CITIZEN. I tell you, whatever famous deeds he's done, he did them for that purpose. Though soft-conscienced men will say he did it for his country, he did it to please his mother and to be partly proud—which he is, right up to the height of his virtue.
SECOND CITIZEN. What he can't help by nature, you call a vice in him. You absolutely can't say he's greedy.

FIRST CITIZEN. If I can't say that, I'm hardly short of accusations. He has faults, with plenty to spare, enough to tire anyone with repeating them. [Shouts within.] What shouts are those? The other side of the city has risen up. Why are we standing here chattering? To the Capitol!
ALL. Come on, come on!
[Menenius Agrippa enters.]
FIRST CITIZEN. Hold on, who's coming here?
SECOND CITIZEN. Worthy Menenius Agrippa, one who's always loved the people.
FIRST CITIZEN. He's honest enough. I wish all the rest were like him!
MENENIUS. What's afoot, my countrymen? Where are you going with bats and clubs? What's the matter? Speak, please.

FIRST CITIZEN. Our business is no secret to the Senate. They've had wind of it for two weeks now—what we mean to do—which we're about to show them in deeds. They say poor petitioners have strong breath; they'll find out we have strong arms too.
MENENIUS. Why, masters, my good friends, my honest neighbours, will you ruin yourselves?
FIRST CITIZEN. We can't, sir; we're ruined already.

MENENIUS. I tell you, friends, the patricians take the most charitable care of you. As for your wants, your suffering in this famine, you might as well strike at the heavens with your sticks as raise them against the Roman state, whose course will continue the way it takes, snapping ten thousand restraints stronger than anything you can put in its way. As for the famine, the gods—not the patricians—cause it, and only your knees, not your arms, can help. Alas, you're carried by calamity to a place where worse awaits you, and you slander the leaders of the state, who care for you like fathers, when you curse them as enemies.

FIRST CITIZEN. Care for us? Sure, that's true! They've never cared for us. They let us starve, while their storehouses are stuffed with grain; they make laws on usury to support usurers; daily they repeal any wholesome act passed against the rich, and daily they pass sharper statutes to chain up and restrain the poor. If the wars don't eat us up, they will; and that's all the love they bear us.

MENENIUS. Either you must confess yourselves astonishingly malicious, or be accused of stupidity. I'll tell you a pretty tale. You may have heard it, but since it serves my purpose, I'll venture to wear it out a little more.
FIRST CITIZEN. Well, I'll hear it, sir; but don't think you can fob off our disgrace with a story. Still, if it pleases you, deliver it.

MENENIUS. There was a time when all the body's members rebelled against the belly, and accused it like this: that it only sat like a gulf in the middle of the body, idle and inactive, always hoarding the food, never doing equal labour with the rest, while the other organs would see and hear, plan, instruct, walk, feel, and, all working together, serve the appetites and needs common to the whole body. The belly answered—
FIRST CITIZEN. Well, sir, what answer did the belly make?

MENENIUS. Sir, I'll tell you. With a kind of smile, which never came from the lungs, but just like this—because, look you, I can make the belly smile as well as speak—it tauntingly replied to the discontented members, the mutinous parts that envied what it received; just as fittingly as you malign our senators because they aren't the same as you.

FIRST CITIZEN. Your belly's answer—what? The kingly crowned head, the watchful eye, the counsellor heart, the arm our soldier, our steed the leg, the tongue our trumpeter, with other defences and small helpers—is this our body, if those—
MENENIUS. What then? Good heavens, this fellow can speak. What then? What then?
FIRST CITIZEN. Should be restrained by the greedy belly, which is the sewer of the body—
MENENIUS. Well, what then?
FIRST CITIZEN. The other organs, if they did complain, what could the belly answer?
MENENIUS. I'll tell you, if you'll grant me a small portion—of what you have little—of patience for a while, you'll hear the belly's answer.
FIRST CITIZEN. You're taking forever about it.

MENENIUS. Note this, good friend: your most solemn belly was deliberate, not rash like its accusers, and answered like this: "True it is, my incorporate friends," said it, "that I receive the general food first, which you live on; and it's right that I do, because I'm the storehouse and the shop of the whole body. But, if you'll remember, I send it through the rivers of your blood right to the court, the heart, to the seat of the brain; and, through the channels and offices of man, the strongest nerves and small inferior veins receive from me the natural sustenance by which they live. And though all at once, you, my good friends"—this says the belly, mark me—
FIRST CITIZEN. Yes, sir, well, well.

MENENIUS. "Though all at once cannot see what I deliver to each one, yet I can balance my accounts, so that all receive back from me the flour of everything, and leave me only the bran." What do you say to that?
FIRST CITIZEN. It was an answer. How do you apply this?

MENENIUS. The senators of Rome are this good belly, and you the mutinous members. For if you examine their counsels and their cares, digest things rightly concerning the common good, you'll find no public benefit you receive that doesn't proceed from them to you, and not at all from yourselves. What do you think, you, the big toe of this assembly?
FIRST CITIZEN. Me, the big toe? Why the big toe?

MENENIUS. Because, being one of the lowest, basest, poorest of this most wise rebellion, you go in the lead. You rascal, you who are worst in blood to lead the run, you take the lead to win some advantage. But get ready your stiff bats and clubs. Rome and her rats are about to do battle; one side or the other must take the punishment.
[Caius Martius enters.]
Hail, noble Martius.
MARTIUS. Thanks.—What's the matter, you quarrelsome rogues, that, rubbing the poor itch of your opinion, make yourselves scabs?
FIRST CITIZEN. We always get your kind words.

MARTIUS. Whoever gives good words to you is flattering below contempt. What do you want, you curs, who like neither peace nor war? The one frightens you; the other makes you proud. Whoever trusts you, where he should find lions, finds hares; where foxes, finds geese. You're no more reliable than the coal of fire on ice, or a hailstone in the sun. Your virtue is to make a worthy man of someone whose offence brings him down, and to curse the justice that did it. Whoever deserves greatness deserves your hate; and your affections are like a sick man's appetite, who craves most what would worsen his disease. He that depends on your favour swims with fins of lead, and chops down oaks with rushes. Hang you all! Trust you? Every minute you change your mind and call him noble whom you just hated, and him vile who was your darling. What's the matter, that in these various places of the city you cry out against the noble senate, who, under the gods, keep you in awe—without which you'd feed on each other?—What are they after?
MENENIUS. They want corn at their own prices, of which they say the city is well stocked.

MARTIUS. Hang them! They say? They'll sit by the fire and pretend to know what's done in the Capitol, who's likely to rise, who thrives and who declines; they take sides in factions and put out speculative marriages, making strong some parties and weakening any that don't stand in their favour beneath their patched shoes. They say there's enough grain? If the nobility would lay aside their pity and let me use my sword, I'd make a heap with thousands of these butchered slaves as high as I could pile my lance.
MENENIUS. Now, these are nearly convinced; for although they grossly lack judgment, they're enormously cowardly. But please, what does the other troop say?

MARTIUS. They've dispersed. Hang them! They said they were hungry, sighed out proverbs that hunger breaks stone walls, that dogs must eat, that meat was made for mouths, that the gods didn't send corn for rich men only. With these scraps they aired their complaints, which being answered and a petition granted them—a strange one, to break the heart of generosity and make bold power look pale—they threw up their caps as if they'd hang them on the horns of the moon, shouting in rivalry.
MENENIUS. What's been granted to them?

MARTIUS. Five tribunes to defend their vulgar wisdom, of their own choosing. One's Junius Brutus, Sicinius Velutus, and I don't know the rest. Damn it! The rabble should have first torn the roofs off the city before they got that out of me. In time it'll erode authority and throw up bigger matters for insurrection to argue over.
MENENIUS. This is strange.
MARTIUS. Go home, you scraps.
[A Messenger enters in haste.]
MESSENGER. Where's Caius Martius?
MARTIUS. Here. What's the matter?
MESSENGER. The news is, sir, the Volsces are in arms.
MARTIUS. I'm glad of it. Then we'll have a way to vent our mouldy surplus.
[Sicinius Velutus, Junius Brutus, two Tribunes; Cominius, Titus Lartius and other Senators enter.]
See, our best elders.
FIRST SENATOR. Martius, what you've recently told us is true: the Volsces are in arms.
MARTIUS. They have a leader, Tullus Aufidius, who'll put you to the test. I sin in envying his nobility, and, were I anything but what I am, I would wish to be only him.
COMINIUS. You've fought together.
MARTIUS. Were half the world at war with the other half and he on my side, I'd defect to make my wars only with him. He's a lion I'm proud to hunt.
FIRST SENATOR. Then, worthy Martius, attend on Cominius in these wars.
COMINIUS. It's your former promise.
MARTIUS. Sir, it is, and I'll stand by it.—Titus Lartius, you'll see me strike at Tullus's face once more. What, are you stiff? Are you holding back?
TITUS LARTIUS. No, Caius Martius, I'll lean on one crutch and fight with the other before I stay behind from this business.
MENENIUS. O, truly bred!
FIRST SENATOR. Your company to the Capitol, where I know our greatest friends are waiting for us.
TITUS LARTIUS. Lead on. [To Cominius.] Follow Cominius. We must follow you; you rightly deserve priority.
COMINIUS. Noble Martius.
FIRST SENATOR.
[To the Citizens.]
Go home, be gone.
MARTIUS. No, let them follow. The Volsces have plenty of corn; take these rats there to gnaw their granaries. Worshipful mutineers, your valour shows itself well. Please follow.
[Exeunt. Sicinius and Brutus remain.]
SICINIUS. Was any man ever as proud as this Martius?
BRUTUS. He has no equal.
SICINIUS. When we were chosen tribunes for the people—
BRUTUS. Did you notice his lip and eyes?
SICINIUS. No, but his taunts.
BRUTUS. When he's stirred, he won't hold back from mocking the gods.
SICINIUS. Mock the modest moon.
BRUTUS. May the present wars devour him! He's grown too proud to be so brave.
SICINIUS. Such a nature, tickled by good success, scorns the shadow it treads on at noon. But I do wonder his insolence can stand being commanded under Cominius.

BRUTUS. Fame, which he aims at, in which he's already well placed, can't be better held or more attained than from a position below the first; for whatever goes wrong will be the General's fault, even if he performs to the utmost of a man, and giddy criticism will then cry out about Martius, "O, if he had run the business!"
SICINIUS. Besides, if things go well, the high opinion that sticks so to Martius will rob Cominius of his deserved credit.
BRUTUS. Come. Half of all Cominius's honours go to Martius, though Martius didn't earn them; and all his faults will be turned to honours for Martius, though indeed he merits no praise in them.
SICINIUS. Let's go and hear how the order is given, and in what manner, beyond his particular role, he goes about this present action.
BRUTUS. Let's go along.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 2 — Corioles. The Senate House
paragraphs: [Tullus Aufidius enters with Senators of Corioles.]
FIRST SENATOR. So your opinion is, Aufidius, that the Romans have got inside our councils and know how we're proceeding.

AUFIDIUS. Isn't it yours? Whatever's been planned in this state that could be brought to action before Rome got around it? It's barely four days since I heard from there. Here are the words—I think I have the letter. Yes, here it is.
[Reads.] They have raised a force, but it isn't known

whether for east or west. The famine is severe. The people are mutinous; and, it's rumoured, Cominius, Martius your old enemy—who's hated worse in Rome than by you—and Titus Lartius, a most valiant Roman, these three lead this preparation, wherever it's headed. Most likely it's for you. Consider it.
FIRST SENATOR. Our army's in the field. We never doubted that Rome was ready to answer us.

AUFIDIUS. Nor did you think it folly to keep your grand intentions veiled until they had to show themselves—which, in the hatching, it seems, were revealed to Rome. By the discovery we'll be cut short in our aim, which was to take many towns before Rome had any idea we were on the move.

SECOND SENATOR. Noble Aufidius, take your commission; hurry to your troops. Leave us to guard Corioles. If they sit down before us, bring up your army to clear them off. But I think you'll find they haven't prepared for us.

AUFIDIUS. O, no doubt of that; I speak from certainties. No, more—some portions of their force are already out, and only headed this way. I take my leave of your Honours. If Caius Martius and I happen to meet, it's sworn between us we'll keep striking until one of us can do no more.
ALL. May the gods help you!
AUFIDIUS. And keep your Honours safe!
FIRST SENATOR. Farewell.
SECOND SENATOR. Farewell.
ALL. Farewell.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 3 — Rome. An apartment in Martius’ house
paragraphs: [Volumnia and Virgilia, mother and wife to Martius, enter. They sit down on two low stools and sew.]

VOLUMNIA. Please, daughter, sing, or carry yourself in a more cheerful way. If my son were my husband, I should rejoice more freely in the absence in which he won honour than in his bed's embraces where he'd show the most love. When he was still just tender-bodied and the only son of my womb, when youth with handsomeness drew all eyes his way, when for a day not even kings' entreaties would have got a mother to sell him an hour from her sight, I—considering how honour would suit such a person, that without it he'd be no better than a portrait hanging on the wall, if renown didn't move him—was pleased to let him seek danger where he was likely to find fame. I sent him to a cruel war, from which he returned with his brows bound in oak. I tell you, daughter, I leapt no more for joy when I first heard he was a man-child than I do now in first seeing he had proved himself a man.
VIRGILIA. But had he died in the business, madam, what then?

VOLUMNIA. Then his good name would have been my son; in that I'd have found my heir. Hear me say sincerely: if I had a dozen sons, each loved alike and none less dear than your dear Martius, I'd rather have eleven die nobly for their country than have one wallow in idle luxury.
[A Gentlewoman enters.]
GENTLEWOMAN. Madam, Lady Valeria has come to visit you.
VIRGILIA. Please, give me leave to withdraw.

VOLUMNIA. Indeed you shall not. I think I hear your husband's drum coming this way; I see him drag Aufidius down by the hair, the Volsces avoiding him as children avoid a bear. I think I see him stamp like this and call like this: "Come on, you cowards! You were conceived in fear, though born in Rome." Wiping his bloody brow with his armoured hand, he goes forth like a harvestman whose job is to mow it all or lose his pay.
VIRGILIA. His bloody brow? O Jupiter, no blood!

VOLUMNIA. Away, you fool! It becomes a man more than gilding becomes his trophy. The breasts of Hecuba, when she suckled Hector, looked no lovelier than Hector's forehead when it spat blood at a Grecian sword in contempt.—Tell Valeria we're ready to welcome her.
[Exit Gentlewoman.]
VIRGILIA. Heaven save my lord from fierce Aufidius!
VOLUMNIA. He'll beat Aufidius's head below his knee and tread on his neck.
[Valeria enters with an Usher and a Gentlewoman.]
VALERIA. My ladies both, good day to you.
VOLUMNIA. Sweet madam.
VIRGILIA. I'm glad to see your Ladyship.
VALERIA. How are you both? You're real homemakers. What are you sewing here? Pretty piece, truly. How is your little son?
VIRGILIA. I thank your Ladyship; well, good madam.
VOLUMNIA. He'd rather see swords and hear a drum than look at his schoolmaster.

VALERIA. Upon my word, his father's son! I'll swear he's a very pretty boy. Upon my honour, I watched him on Wednesday for a whole half hour. He has such a determined look. I saw him chase a gilded butterfly, and when he caught it, he let it go again, and chased it again, and over and over he comes, and up again, catching it again. Whether his fall enraged him or how it was, he set his teeth and tore it. O, I'll warrant how he mangled it!
VOLUMNIA. Just like one of his father's moods.
VALERIA. Indeed, truly, he's a noble child.
VIRGILIA. A lively one, madam.
VALERIA. Come, set aside your sewing. I must have you play the idle housewife with me this afternoon.
VIRGILIA. No, good madam, I won't go outside.
VALERIA. Not outside?
VOLUMNIA. She shall, she shall.
VIRGILIA. Indeed, no, by your patience. I won't cross the threshold till my lord returns from the wars.
VALERIA. For shame, you confine yourself most unreasonably. Come, you must go visit the good lady who's just given birth.
VIRGILIA. I'll wish her speedy strength and visit her in my prayers, but I can't go there.
VOLUMNIA. Why, please?
VIRGILIA. It's not to save effort, nor because I lack love.

VALERIA. You'd be another Penelope. Yet they say all the yarn she spun during Ulysses's absence only filled Ithaca with moths. Come, I wish your linen had as much feeling as your finger, so you'd stop pricking it for pity. Come, you must go with us.
VIRGILIA. No, good madam, pardon me; indeed, I won't go out.
VALERIA. Truly, come with me, and I'll tell you excellent news about your husband.
VIRGILIA. O, good madam, there can't be any yet.
VALERIA. Truly, I'm not joking with you. News came from him last night.
VIRGILIA. Indeed, madam!

VALERIA. In earnest, it's true. I heard a senator say it. This is what it is: the Volsces have an army out, against whom Cominius the General has gone with one part of our Roman force. Your lord and Titus Lartius have set down before their city Corioles. They have no doubt of prevailing, and of making it a brief war. This is true, on my honour, and so, please, go with us.
VIRGILIA. Give me excuse, good madam. I'll obey you in everything from now on.
VOLUMNIA. Leave her alone, lady. As she is now, she'd only spoil our better mirth.
VALERIA. Truly, I think she would.—Fare you well, then.—Come, good sweet lady.—Please, Virgilia, turn your solemness out of doors, and come along with us.
VIRGILIA. No, in a word, madam. Indeed I must not. I wish you much mirth.
VALERIA. Well then, farewell.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 4 — Before Corioles
paragraphs: [Martius and Titus Lartius enter, with drum and colours, with Captains and Soldiers, as before the city of Corioles. A Messenger comes to them.]
MARTIUS. Here comes news. A wager they've met.
LARTIUS. My horse against yours, no.
MARTIUS. Done.
LARTIUS. Agreed.
MARTIUS.
[To Messenger.] Tell us, has our general met the enemy?
MESSENGER. They lie in sight but haven't engaged yet.
LARTIUS. So the good horse is mine.
MARTIUS. I'll buy him from you.
LARTIUS. No, I'll neither sell nor give him. But I'll lend him to you for half a hundred years.—Summon the town.
MARTIUS. How far off do these armies lie?
MESSENGER. Within a mile and a half.
MARTIUS. Then we shall hear their alarum, and they ours. Now, Mars, please, make our work quick, so we with smoking swords can march from here to help our friends in the field!—Come, blow your blast.
[They sound a parley.]
[Two Senators enter with others on the walls of Corioles.]
Tullus Aufidius—is he within your walls?
FIRST SENATOR. No, nor any man that fears you less than he: that's less than a little.
[Drum afar off.]
Listen, our drums are bringing out our youth. We'll break our own walls rather than be penned in. Our gates, which seem shut, we've only pinned with rushes. They'll open by themselves.
[Alarum far off.]
Listen, far off! That's Aufidius. Hear what work he makes among your split army.
MARTIUS. O, they're at it!
LARTIUS. Their noise be our cue.—Ladders, ho!
[The Volscian Army enters as through the city gates.]

MARTIUS. They don't fear us; they're coming out of their city.—Now put your shields in front of your hearts, and fight with hearts harder than shields.—Forward, brave Titus. They disdain us far more than we'd thought, which makes me sweat with rage.—Come on, my fellows! Whoever retreats, I'll take him for a Volsce, and he shall feel my blade.
[Alarums. The Romans are beaten back to their trenches. They exit, with the Volsces following.]
[Martius enters cursing, with Roman soldiers.]

MARTIUS. All the plagues of the south land on you, you shames of Rome! You herd of—boils and pestilence plaster you over, so you may be loathed beyond mere sight, and one infect another against the wind a mile! You souls of geese, who wear the shapes of men, how have you run from slaves that apes could beat! Pluto and hell! All wounds in the back. Backs red, and faces pale with flight and fever-shaking fear! Mend yourselves, and charge home, or, by the fires of heaven, I'll leave the foe and make my wars on you. See to it. Come on! If you stand fast, we'll beat them back to their wives, just as they drove us to our trenches. Follow me!
[Another alarum. The Volsces re-enter and are driven back to the gates of Corioles, which open to let them in.]
So, now the gates are open. Now prove yourselves good seconds! Fortune widens them for the pursuers, not for those who flee. Watch me, and do the same.
[Martius follows the fleeing Volsces through the gates, and is shut in.]
FIRST SOLDIER. Foolhardiness, not me.
SECOND SOLDIER. Nor me.
FIRST SOLDIER. Look, they've shut him in.
[Alarum continues.]
ALL. He's done for, I'll wager.
[Titus Lartius enters.]
LARTIUS. What's become of Martius?
ALL. Slain, sir, no doubt.
FIRST SOLDIER. Following the fleeing Volsces right at their heels, he entered with them; who suddenly slammed shut their gates. He's all alone, facing the whole city.

LARTIUS. O noble fellow, who sensibly outdares his senseless sword, and stands up when it bends! You are left behind, Martius. A whole ruby, as big as you are, wouldn't be so rich a jewel. You were a soldier even to Cato's ideal—not fierce and terrible only in strokes, but with your grim looks and the thunder-like percussion of your sounds you made your enemies shake, as if the world were feverous and trembled.
[Martius enters, bleeding, assaulted by the enemy.]
FIRST SOLDIER. Look, sir.
LARTIUS. O, it's Martius! Let's fetch him out or perish with him.
[They fight, and all enter the city.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 5 — Within Corioles. A street
paragraphs: [Certain Romans enter, with spoils.]
FIRST ROMAN. This I'll carry to Rome.
SECOND ROMAN. And I this.
THIRD ROMAN. Damn it! I took this for silver.
[Martius and Titus Lartius enter with a Trumpet.]

MARTIUS. Look at these scavengers who value their time at a cracked drachma. Cushions, lead spoons, iron worth a farthing, jackets that hangmen would bury with the men who wore them—these base slaves, before the fight is even over, are packing up. Down with them!
[Exit the Romans with spoils.]
[Alarum continues still afar off.]

And listen, what noise the General is making! Onward to him! There's the man my soul hates, Aufidius, cutting through our Romans. So, valiant Titus, take enough men to hold the city, while I, with those who have the spirit, will hurry to help Cominius.
LARTIUS. Worthy sir, you're bleeding. Your exertion has been too violent for a second round of fight.
MARTIUS. Sir, don't praise me. My work hasn't even warmed me up yet. Farewell. The blood I drop is more medicinal than dangerous to me. Like this I'll appear to Aufidius and fight him.
LARTIUS. Now may the fair goddess Fortune fall deep in love with you, and may her great charms misguide your opponents' swords! Bold gentleman, may prosperity attend you!
MARTIUS. Your friend no less than those she places highest! So farewell.
LARTIUS. You worthiest Martius!
[Exit Martius.]
Go sound your trumpet in the marketplace. Call all the officers of the town there, where they'll learn our intentions. Away!
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 6 — Near the camp of Cominius
paragraphs: [Cominius enters as if in retreat, with Soldiers.]

COMINIUS. Catch your breath, my friends. Well fought! We've come off like Romans, neither foolish in our stands nor cowardly in retreat. Believe me, sirs, we shall be charged again. While we've been fighting, in lulls and on shifting gusts of wind we've heard the charges of our friends. May the Roman gods lead their successes as we wish our own, so that both our forces, meeting with smiling faces, may offer up grateful sacrifice!
[A Messenger enters.]
Your news?
MESSENGER. The citizens of Corioles have come out and given battle to Lartius and Martius. I saw our side driven to their trenches, and then I came away.
COMINIUS. Though you speak the truth, I think you don't speak well of it. How long ago was this?
MESSENGER. Over an hour, my lord.
COMINIUS. It's not a mile away; we heard their drums only briefly. How could you take an hour to cover a mile and bring your news so late?
MESSENGER. Spies of the Volsces held me in chase, so I was forced to wheel three or four miles about; otherwise, sir, I'd have brought my report half an hour ago.
[Exit Messenger.]
[Martius enters, bloody.]
COMINIUS. Who's that, who looks as though he'd been flayed? O gods, he has the stamp of Martius, and I've seen him this way before.
MARTIUS. Have I come too late?
COMINIUS. The shepherd can no more tell thunder from a tabor than I can mistake the sound of Martius's tongue for any lesser man's.
MARTIUS. Have I come too late?
COMINIUS. Yes, if you come covered not in the blood of others, but cloaked in your own.
MARTIUS. O, let me embrace you in arms as sound as when I wooed, with a heart as merry as when our wedding day was done and the candles burned us to bed!
COMINIUS. Flower of warriors, how does Titus Lartius fare?

MARTIUS. Like a man busy with decrees—condemning some to death and some to exile; ransoming or pitying one, threatening the other; holding Corioles in Rome's name like a fawning greyhound on a leash, to slip at will.
COMINIUS. Where's that slave who told me they'd beaten you back to your trenches? Where is he? Call him here.

MARTIUS. Leave him alone. He told the truth. But as for our gentlemen, the common rank—a plague on them! Tribunes for them!—the mouse never shunned the cat as they ran from rascals worse than they were.
COMINIUS. But how did you prevail?
MARTIUS. Will time allow me to tell? I don't think so. Where's the enemy? Are you masters of the field? If not, why are you stopping until you are?
COMINIUS. Martius, we've fought at a disadvantage, and retreated to win our objective.
MARTIUS. How is their battle line laid out? Do you know on which side they've placed their most trusted men?
COMINIUS. As I guess, Martius, their bands in the vanguard are the Antiates, their best trust; over them is Aufidius, the very heart of their hope.

MARTIUS. I beg you, by all the battles we have fought in, by the blood we have shed together, by the vows we have made to remain friends, that you set me directly against Aufidius and his Antiates, and that you not delay the present, but, filling the air with raised swords and darts, that we prove ourselves this very hour.
COMINIUS. Though I'd wish you were taken to a gentle bath and balms applied to you, I dare not deny what you ask. Take your pick of those who can best aid your action.

MARTIUS. Those are they who are most willing. If any such are here—as it would be a sin to doubt—who love this painting in which you see me smeared; if any fear losing his life less than a bad reputation; if any think brave death outweighs a bad life, and that his country is dearer than himself; let him alone, or as many as feel that way, wave like this to show his disposition and follow Martius.
[He waves his sword.]
[They all shout and wave their swords, lift him up in their arms, and cast up their caps.]

O, me alone! Will you make a sword of me? If these gestures aren't merely outward, which of you isn't worth four Volsces? Not one of you but can bear against the great Aufidius a shield as tough as his. A certain number—though thanks to all—I must select from all. The rest shall play their part in some other fight, as the cause demands. Please march, and I'll quickly draw out my command of those best disposed.
COMINIUS. March on, my fellows. Live up to this display, and you'll share equally with us in everything.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 7 — The gates of Corioles
paragraphs: [Titus Lartius, having set a guard on Corioles, going with drum and trumpet toward Cominius and Caius Martius, enters with a Lieutenant, other Soldiers, and a Scout.]

LARTIUS. So, let the gates be guarded. Keep your duties as I've laid them down. If I send for help, dispatch those companies to our aid; the rest will serve to hold for a short time. If we lose the field, we can't keep the town.
LIEUTENANT. Don't worry about our diligence, sir.
LARTIUS. Off you go, and shut your gates behind us. Our guide, come. Lead us to the Roman camp.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 8 — A field of battle between the Roman and the Volscian camps
paragraphs: [Alarum, as in battle. Martius and Aufidius enter at separate doors.]
MARTIUS. I'll fight no one but you, for I hate you worse than a promise-breaker.
AUFIDIUS. We hate alike. Africa owns no serpent I loathe more than your fame and envy of you. Plant your foot.
MARTIUS. May the first to retreat die the other's slave, and the gods damn him afterward!
AUFIDIUS. If I flee, Martius, holler after me like at a hare.

MARTIUS. Within these three hours, Tullus, alone I fought inside your Corioles' walls, and did whatever work I pleased. It isn't my blood you see me masked in. For your revenge, screw up your strength to its highest pitch.
AUFIDIUS. Were you the Hector that was the scourge of your boasted lineage, you shouldn't escape me here.
[Here they fight, and certain Volsces come to the aid of Aufidius.]
Officious and not valiant—you've shamed me with your condemned interference.
[Martius fights till they are driven in breathless. Aufidius and Martius exit, separately.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 9 — The Roman camp
paragraphs: [Alarum. A retreat is sounded. Flourish. At one door, Cominius enters with the Romans; at another door, Martius, with his arm in a scarf.]

COMINIUS. If I were to recount today's work to you, you wouldn't believe your own deeds. But I'll report it where senators will mix tears with smiles; where great patricians will listen and shrug, and in the end admire; where ladies will be frightened and, joyfully shaken, ask to hear more; where the dull tribunes, who along with the musty plebeians hate your honours, will say against their hearts, "We thank the gods our Rome has such a soldier." Yet you came to only a morsel of this feast, having dined fully before.
[Titus Lartius enters with his force, from the pursuit.]
LARTIUS. O general, here is the steed, and we the trappings. Had you only seen—

MARTIUS. Please, no more. My mother, who has a licence to extol her blood, when she praises me grieves me. I've done as you have done—that's all I can; driven as you have been—that's for my country. Whoever has only carried out his good will has matched what I did.

COMINIUS. You shall not be the grave of your own merit. Rome must know the value of her own. It would be a concealment worse than theft, no less than a slander, to hide your doings and to silence what, voiced to the highest peak of praise, would still seem modest. Therefore, I beg you—as a sign of what you are, not as reward for what you've done—before our army hear me.
MARTIUS. I have some wounds on me, and they smart to hear themselves recalled.

COMINIUS. If they didn't, they might well fester against ingratitude and dress themselves with death. Of all the horses—of which we've taken a good many, and good ones—of all the treasure won on this field and from the city, we offer you the tenth, to be taken out before the general distribution, at your sole choice.
MARTIUS. I thank you, general, but I can't make my heart consent to take a bribe to pay my sword. I refuse it; and stand on my common share with those who saw the doing.
[A long flourish. They all cry "Martius, Martius!" and cast up their caps and lances. Cominius and Lartius stand bare-headed.]

May these same instruments, which you're now profaning, never sound again! When drums and trumpets become flatterers in the field, let courts and cities be made all of false-faced flattery! When steel grows soft as the parasite's silk, let him be made an ovator of the wars! No more, I say. Just because I haven't washed my bleeding nose, or beaten down some feeble wretch—which many others here have done, unnoticed—you shout me forth in exaggerated acclamations, as if I loved my modesty to be fed on praises seasoned with lies.

COMINIUS. You're too modest, more cruel to your own reputation than grateful to us who give it truly. By your patience, if you're enraged against yourself, we'll put you in manacles, like one who intends his own harm, then reason safely with you. Therefore let it be known to us and to all the world that Caius Martius wears this war's garland, in token of which I give him my noble steed, known to the camp, with all his trappings. And from this time, for what he did before Corioles, call him, with all the applause and clamour of the army, Caius Martius Coriolanus! Bear the added name nobly forever!
[Flourish. Trumpets sound, and drums.]
ALL. Caius Martius Coriolanus!

CORIOLANUS. I'll go wash; and when my face is clean, you'll see whether I blush or not. Nevertheless, I thank you. I mean to ride your horse, and at all times to live up to your kind addition, to the fullness of my power.

COMINIUS. So, to our tent—where, before we rest, we'll write to Rome about our success.—You, Titus Lartius, must go back to Corioles. Send us to Rome the best of them, with whom we may negotiate for their good and ours.
LARTIUS. I shall, my lord.
CORIOLANUS. The gods are starting to mock me. I, who just refused most princely gifts, am forced to beg of my lord general.
COMINIUS. Take it, it's yours. What is it?

CORIOLANUS. I once lay here in Corioles at a poor man's house; he treated me kindly. He cried out to me; I saw him a prisoner; but then Aufidius was within my view, and rage overwhelmed my pity. I ask you to grant my poor host freedom.
COMINIUS. O, well begged! Were he the butcher of my son, he should be free as the wind.—Release him, Titus.
LARTIUS. Martius, what's his name?
CORIOLANUS. By Jupiter, forgotten! I'm weary; yes, my memory is tired. Have we no wine here?
COMINIUS. Let's go to our tent. The blood on your face is drying; it's time it was tended to. Come.
[A flourish of cornets. Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 10 — The camp of the Volsces
paragraphs: [A flourish. Cornets. Tullus Aufidius enters, bloody, with two or three soldiers.]
AUFIDIUS. The town is taken.
SOLDIER. It will be handed back on favourable terms.

AUFIDIUS. Terms? I wish I were a Roman, for as a Volsce I can't be what I am. Terms? What good terms can a treaty find on the side that's at mercy? Five times, Martius, I've fought with you; that often you've beaten me, and would do so, I think, if we met as often as we eat. By the elements, if ever again I meet him face to face, he's mine or I am his. My rivalry has lost the honour it once had; for where I thought to crush him on equal terms, true sword against sword, I'll strike at him by any means—wrath or craft may take him.
SOLDIER. He's the devil.

AUFIDIUS. Bolder, though not so subtle. My valour is poisoned with the stain it suffers from him alone; for him it will fly out of itself. Neither sleep nor sanctuary, naked or sick, neither temple nor Capitol, the prayers of priests nor times of sacrifice—those embargoes against fury—shall lift up their rotten privilege and custom against my hate of Martius. Wherever I find him—were it at home, under my brother's protection—even there, against the law of hospitality, I'd wash my fierce hand in his heart. Go to the city; learn how it's held and who must be hostages for Rome.
SOLDIER. Won't you come?
AUFIDIUS. I'm expected at the cypress grove. Please—it's south of the city mills—bring me word there how things go, so I can spur my journey at its pace.
SOLDIER. I shall, sir.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 1 — Rome. A public place
paragraphs: [Menenius enters with the two Tribunes of the people, Sicinius and Brutus.]
MENENIUS. The augur tells me we shall have news tonight.
BRUTUS. Good or bad?
MENENIUS. Not according to the people's prayers, for they don't love Martius.
SICINIUS. Nature teaches beasts to know their friends.
MENENIUS. Tell me, please, who does the wolf love?
SICINIUS. The lamb.
MENENIUS. Yes, to devour him, as the hungry plebeians would devour the noble Martius.
BRUTUS. He's a lamb indeed, who bleats like a bear.
MENENIUS. He's a bear indeed, who lives like a lamb. You two are old men; answer me one thing I'll ask you.
BOTH TRIBUNES. Well, sir.
MENENIUS. In what enormity is Martius lacking, that you two haven't in abundance?
BRUTUS. He's lacking in no single fault, but stocked with all of them.
SICINIUS. Especially in pride.
BRUTUS. And surpassing all others in boasting.
MENENIUS. This is strange now. Do you two know how you're judged here in the city—I mean by us on the patrician side—do you?
BOTH TRIBUNES. Why, how are we judged?
MENENIUS. Since you're talking about pride now, won't you get angry?
BOTH TRIBUNES. Well, well, sir, go on?

MENENIUS. Why, it's no great matter; for a very small thief of opportunity will rob you of a great deal of patience. Let your tempers loose, and be angry at your pleasure—at least, if you take being so as a pleasure. You blame Martius for being proud.
BRUTUS. We're not the only ones, sir.

MENENIUS. I know you can do very little alone, for your helpers are many; otherwise, your actions would shrink to almost nothing. Your abilities are too infantile for doing much alone. You talk of pride. O, if only you could turn your eyes toward the napes of your necks and make even a small interior survey of your good selves! O, if only you could!
BOTH TRIBUNES. What then, sir?
MENENIUS. Why, then you'd discover a pair of unworthy, proud, violent, irritable magistrates—alias fools, as any in Rome.
SICINIUS. Menenius, you're well known too.

MENENIUS. I'm known to be a humorous patrician, and one who loves a cup of hot wine with not a drop of diluting Tiber water in it; said to be somewhat flawed in favouring the first complaint, hasty and tinder-like over too trivial a cause; one who keeps more company with the back end of the night than with the forehead of the morning. What I think I say, and I spend my malice in my breath. Meeting two such statesmen as you are—I can hardly call you Lycurguses—if the drink you give me hits my palate badly, I make a sour face at it. I can't say your Worships have delivered the matter well when I find the ass in compound with the major part of your syllables. And though I must be content to put up with those who say you are reverend grave men, yet they lie outright who tell you that you have good faces. If you see this in the map of my microcosm, does it follow that I'm well known too? What harm can your bleary perceptions glean from this character of me, if I'm well known too?
BRUTUS. Come, sir, come; we know you well enough.

MENENIUS. You know neither me, nor yourselves, nor anything. You're ambitious for poor knaves' caps and bows. You waste a good wholesome morning hearing a case between an orange-seller and a faucet-seller, and then adjourn the dispute over threepence to a second day of audience. When you're hearing a matter between party and party, if you happen to be pinched with colic, you make faces like mummers, raise the bloody flag against all patience, and, while roaring for a chamber pot, dismiss the dispute bleeding and more tangled by your hearing. All the peace you achieve in their cause is calling both parties knaves. You're a pair of strange ones.
BRUTUS. Come, come. You're well understood to be a better jester for the dinner table than a useful member of the Capitol's bench.

MENENIUS. Our very priests must become mockers if they encounter such ridiculous subjects as you. When you speak best to the point, it isn't worth the wagging of your beards, and your beards don't deserve so honourable a grave as to stuff a tailor's cushion or be entombed in a donkey's packsaddle. Yet you must keep saying Martius is proud, who, at the cheapest estimate, is worth all your predecessors since Deucalion—though some of the best of them may have been hereditary hangmen. Good evening to your Worships. More of your conversation would infect my brain, you being the herdsmen of the beastly plebeians. I will boldly take my leave.
[He begins to exit. Brutus and Sicinius stand aside.]
[Volumnia, Virgilia and Valeria enter.]
How now, my as fair as noble ladies—and the moon, if she were earthly, no nobler—where are you following your eyes so fast?
VOLUMNIA. Honourable Menenius, my boy Martius is approaching. For the love of Juno, let's go!
MENENIUS. Ha? Martius coming home?
VOLUMNIA. Yes, worthy Menenius, and with the most prosperous approbation.
MENENIUS. Take my cap, Jupiter, and I thank you! Hoo! Martius coming home?
VALERIA, VIRGILIA. No, it's true.
VOLUMNIA. Look, here's a letter from him. The state has another, his wife another, and I think there's one at home for you.
MENENIUS. I'll make my very house reel tonight. A letter for me?
VIRGILIA. Yes, certainly, there's a letter for you; I saw it.

MENENIUS. A letter for me? It gives me an estate of seven years' health, during which time I'll make a face at the physician. The most sovereign prescription in Galen is just empirical quackery and, compared to this preservative, of no better repute than a horse drench. Isn't he wounded? He used to come home wounded.
VIRGILIA. O, no, no, no!
VOLUMNIA. O, he is wounded, I thank the gods for it.
MENENIUS. So do I too, if it isn't too much. Does he bring victory in his pocket? Then the wounds suit him.
VOLUMNIA. On his brows, Menenius. He comes home the third time with the oak garland.
MENENIUS. Has he disciplined Aufidius soundly?
VOLUMNIA. Titus Lartius writes that they fought together, but Aufidius got away.
MENENIUS. And it was time for him too, I'll warrant. If he'd stayed by him, I wouldn't have been so 'fidiused for all the chests in Corioles and all the gold in them. Is the Senate apprised of this?
VOLUMNIA. Good ladies, let's go.—Yes, yes, yes. The Senate has letters from the General, in which he gives my son the whole credit for the war. He has in this action doubly outdone his former deeds.
VALERIA. Truly, wondrous things are being said of him.
MENENIUS. Wondrous? Yes, I warrant you, and not without his truly earning them.
VIRGILIA. May the gods grant them true.
VOLUMNIA. True? Pow, waw!
MENENIUS. True? I'll swear they're true. Where is he wounded? [To the Tribunes.] God save your good Worships! Martius is coming home; he has more reason to be proud.—Where is he wounded?
VOLUMNIA. In the shoulder and in the left arm. There will be large scars to show the people when he stands for his place. He received seven wounds in the body in the repulse of Tarquin.
MENENIUS. One in the neck and two in the thigh—that's nine that I know of.
VOLUMNIA. He had, before this last expedition, twenty-five wounds on him.
MENENIUS. Now it's twenty-seven. Every gash was an enemy's grave.
[A shout and flourish.]
Listen, the trumpets!
VOLUMNIA. These are Martius's ushers: before him he carries noise, and behind him he leaves tears. Death, that dark spirit, lies in his sinewy arm, which, being raised, falls, and then men die.
[A sennet.]
[Cominius the General and Titus Lartius enter, between them Coriolanus crowned with an oak garland, with Captains and Soldiers and a Herald. Trumpets sound.]
HERALD. Know, Rome, that all alone Martius fought within Corioles's gates, where he has won, with fame, a name for Caius Martius; these honours add "Coriolanus." Welcome to Rome, renowned Coriolanus.
[Sound flourish.]
ALL. Welcome to Rome, renowned Coriolanus!
CORIOLANUS. No more of this, it offends my heart. Please, no more.
COMINIUS. Look, sir, your mother.
CORIOLANUS. O, you have, I know, petitioned all the gods for my prosperity.
[Kneels.]
VOLUMNIA. No, my good soldier, up.
[He stands.]
My gentle Martius, worthy Caius, and newly named by deed-achieving honour—what is it? Must I call you Coriolanus? But, O, your wife—

CORIOLANUS. My gracious silence, hail. Would you have laughed if I'd come home in a coffin, you who weep to see me triumph? Ah, my dear, such eyes the widows in Corioles wear, and mothers who have lost sons.
MENENIUS. Now may the gods crown you!
CORIOLANUS. And you're still alive? [To Valeria.] O my sweet lady, pardon.
VOLUMNIA. I don't know where to turn. O, welcome home! And welcome, general.—And you're all welcome.

MENENIUS. A hundred thousand welcomes! I could weep, and I could laugh; I am light and heavy. Welcome. A curse take root at the very heart of anyone who isn't glad to see you! You are three whom Rome should dote on; yet, by my faith, we have some old crab trees here at home that won't be grafted to your taste. Yet welcome, warriors! We call a nettle just a nettle, and the faults of fools just folly.
COMINIUS. Always right.
CORIOLANUS. Menenius always, always.
HERALD. Make way there, and proceed!
CORIOLANUS.
[To Volumnia and Virgilia.] Your hand, and yours.
Before I shade my head in our own house, the good patricians must be visited, from whom I've received not only greetings, but with them a change of honours.
VOLUMNIA. I've lived to see my very wishes inherited and the buildings of my fancy realised. There's only one thing wanting, which I have no doubt our Rome will cast upon you.
CORIOLANUS. Know, good mother, I'd rather be their servant in my way than rule them in theirs.
COMINIUS. On, to the Capitol.
[Flourish of cornets. Exeunt in state, as before.]
[Brutus and Sicinius come forward.]

BRUTUS. All tongues speak of him, and the bleary-eyed put on spectacles to see him. Your chattering nurse lets her baby scream itself into a fit while she gossips about him. The kitchen wench pins her best linen around her grimy neck, climbing the walls to see him. Stalls, market booths, windows are packed; rooftops filled, and ridge-poles straddled by people of every complexion, all agreeing in their eagerness to see him. Rarely-seen priests press into the popular throngs and push to win a common standing-place. Our veiled ladies expose the war of white and pink in their carefully-painted cheeks to the wanton spoil of Phoebus's burning kisses. Such a commotion, as if whichever god leads him had slyly crept into his human powers and given him graceful bearing.
SICINIUS. He'll be made consul on the spot, I warrant.
BRUTUS. Then our office may, while his power lasts, go sleep.
SICINIUS. He can't carry his honours temperately from where he should begin to where he should end, but will lose those he's won.
BRUTUS. In that there's comfort.

SICINIUS. Don't doubt the commoners, for whom we stand—they, with their old animosity, will at the slightest cause forget these his new honours; and that he'll give them cause is as little in doubt as that he's proud enough to do it.

BRUTUS. I heard him swear that, were he to stand for consul, he'd never appear in the marketplace nor put on the napless robe of humility, nor show, as the custom is, his wounds to the people, to beg their stinking breaths.
SICINIUS. That's right.
BRUTUS. It was his word. O, he'd miss it rather than carry it by anything but the gentry's suit to him and the desire of the nobles.
SICINIUS. I want nothing better than to have him hold that purpose and put it in execution.
BRUTUS. It's most likely he will.
SICINIUS. It shall then be to him, as we wish, a sure destruction.

BRUTUS. So it must turn out, either for him or for our authority, in the end. We must suggest to the people in what hatred he has always held them; that with his power he would have made them mules, silenced their pleaders, and stripped them of their freedoms; holding them in human action and capacity as having no more soul nor fitness for the world than camels in their war, who get their feed only for bearing burdens, and sore blows for sinking under them.

SICINIUS. This, as you say, suggested at some time when his soaring insolence touches the people—and that time won't be lacking, if it's set up, which is as easy as setting dogs on sheep—will be his fire to kindle their dry stubble, and their blaze will darken him forever.
[A Messenger enters.]
BRUTUS. What's the matter?

MESSENGER. You're sent for to the Capitol. It's thought that Martius shall be consul. I've seen the dumb crowd to see him, and the blind to hear him speak; matrons threw gloves, ladies and maids their scarves and handkerchiefs, upon him as he passed; the nobles bowed as to Jove's statue, and the commoners made a shower and thunder with their caps and shouts. I never saw the like.
BRUTUS. Let's to the Capitol; and carry with us ears and eyes for the moment, but hearts for the outcome.
SICINIUS. I'll come with you.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 2 — Rome. The Capitol
paragraphs: [Two Officers enter, to lay cushions, as if in the Capitol.]
FIRST OFFICER. Come, come. They're almost here. How many are standing for consul?
SECOND OFFICER. Three, they say; but everyone thinks Coriolanus will carry it.
FIRST OFFICER. That's a brave fellow, but he's frightfully proud and doesn't love the common people.

SECOND OFFICER. Truly, there have been many great men who have flattered the people while never loving them; and there are many they've loved without knowing why; so that, if they love without knowing why, they hate on no better ground. Therefore, for Coriolanus not to care whether they love or hate him shows the true knowledge he has of their disposition, and out of his noble carelessness, he lets them plainly see it.

FIRST OFFICER. If he didn't care whether he had their love or not, he'd be indifferent between doing them neither good nor harm; but he seeks their hate with greater devotion than they can offer it to him, and leaves nothing undone that may fully prove him their opposite. Now, to appear to court the malice and displeasure of the people is as bad as the thing he dislikes—flattering them for their love.

SECOND OFFICER. He has deserved well of his country, and his rise hasn't been by such easy steps as those who, having been pliant and courteous to the people, cap in hand, with no further deed bring themselves wholly into their estimation and report; rather, he has so planted his honours in their eyes and his actions in their hearts that for their tongues to be silent and not confess as much would be a kind of ungrateful injury. To report otherwise would be a malice that, contradicting itself, would draw reproof and rebuke from every ear that heard it.
FIRST OFFICER. No more of him; he's a worthy man. Make way. They're coming.

[A sennet. The Patricians and the Tribunes of the people enter, Lictors before them; Coriolanus, Menenius, Cominius the consul. The Patricians sit. Sicinius and Brutus take their places by themselves. Coriolanus stands.]

MENENIUS. Having decided about the Volsces and to send for Titus Lartius, the main business of this our follow-up meeting is to honour his noble service in standing up for his country. So please, most reverend and grave elders, ask the present consul and recent general to report on a little of that worthy work performed by Martius Caius Coriolanus, whom we met here both to thank and to remember with honours befitting him.
[Coriolanus sits.]

FIRST SENATOR. Speak, good Cominius. Leave nothing out for the sake of brevity, and make us think rather that our state's lacking in repayment than that we'd stretch it out. Masters of the people, we ask your kindest ears, and after, your loving recommendation to the common body to grant what passes here.
SICINIUS. We are assembled for a pleasing matter, and have hearts inclined to honour and advance the theme of our gathering.
BRUTUS. Which we'll be all the more glad to do if he'll remember a kinder estimation of the people than he has previously held them in.
MENENIUS. That's off the point, that's off! I wish you'd kept silent. Are you willing to hear Cominius speak?
BRUTUS. Most willingly. But still my caution was more pertinent than the rebuke you give it.
MENENIUS. He loves your people, but don't tie him to be their bedfellow.—Worthy Cominius, speak.
[Coriolanus rises, and tries to go away.]
No, keep your seat.
FIRST SENATOR. Sit, Coriolanus. Never be ashamed to hear what you've nobly done.
CORIOLANUS. Your Honours, pardon me. I'd rather have my wounds heal over again than hear told how I got them.
BRUTUS. Sir, I hope my words didn't drive you off the bench?

CORIOLANUS. No, sir. Yet often, when blows have made me stand my ground, I've fled from words. You didn't soothe me, therefore you didn't hurt me; but your people, I love them as much as they're worth.
MENENIUS. Please now, sit down.
CORIOLANUS. I'd rather have someone scratch my head in the sun while the alarm sounded than sit idly to hear my nothings monstered into great things.
[Exit.]

MENENIUS. Masters of the people, your multiplying brood—how can he flatter them, when it's a thousand bad ones to one good one—when you now see he'd rather risk all his limbs for honour than risk one of his ears to hear it?—Proceed, Cominius.

COMINIUS. I shall lack voice. The deeds of Coriolanus should not be uttered feebly. It's held that valour is the chief virtue and most dignifies the one who has it; if so, the man I speak of cannot in the world be singly counterbalanced. At sixteen years, when Tarquin made a thrust at Rome, he fought beyond the standard of others. Our dictator then, whom with all praise I point at, saw him fight when with his beardless chin he drove the bristled lips before him. He bestrode an overpowered Roman and in the Consul's view slew three opponents. He met Tarquin himself and struck him to his knee. In that day's feats, when he might have played the woman in the scene, he proved the best man in the field, and for his reward was brow-crowned with oak. Having entered manhood in his pupil age, he grew like a sea, and in the brunt of seventeen battles since, he beat all swords to the garland. For this last action, before and in Corioles, let me say, I cannot do him full justice. He stopped the fleeing Romans, and by his rare example made cowards turn terror into sport. As weeds part before a vessel under sail, so men obeyed and fell beneath his stem. His sword, Death's stamp, where it marked, it took; from face to foot he was a thing of blood, whose every motion was timed by dying cries. Alone he entered the mortal gate of the city, which he painted with inescapable destiny; without aid he came off, and with sudden reinforcement struck Corioles like a planet. Now all's his, when suddenly the din of war pierced his ready senses; then immediately his doubled spirit revived what in flesh was exhausted, and to battle he came, where he ran reeking over the lives of men as if it were a perpetual spoil; and until we called both field and city ours, he never stopped to ease his chest with panting.
MENENIUS. Worthy man!
FIRST SENATOR. He can only with adequacy fit the honours we devise for him.

COMINIUS. Our spoils he kicked aside; and he looked on precious things as if they were the common muck of the world. He desires less than misery itself would give, rewards his deeds with the doing of them, and is content to spend the time to end it.
MENENIUS. He's truly noble. Let him be called for.
FIRST SENATOR. Call Coriolanus.
OFFICER. He appears.
[Coriolanus enters.]
MENENIUS. The Senate, Coriolanus, is well pleased to make you consul.
CORIOLANUS. I still owe them my life and services.
MENENIUS. Then it remains for you to speak to the people.
CORIOLANUS. I beg you, let me skip that custom, for I can't put on the gown, stand bare, and beg them, for my wounds' sake, to give their votes. Please let me pass over this doing.
SICINIUS. Sir, the people must have their say; they won't drop one jot of ceremony.
MENENIUS. Don't push them to it. Please, go and conform to the custom, and take to yourself, as your predecessors have, your honour with its proper form.
CORIOLANUS. It's a role I'll blush to act in, and one that might well be taken from the people.
BRUTUS. Did you mark that?
CORIOLANUS. To brag to them, "thus I did, and thus!" Show them the painless scars I should hide, as if I'd received them only for the hire of their breath!
MENENIUS. Don't insist on this.—We commend to you, tribunes of the people, our purpose toward them, and to our noble consul we all wish joy and honour.
SENATORS. May all joy and honour come to Coriolanus!
[Flourish of cornets. Exeunt all but Sicinius and Brutus.]
BRUTUS. You see how he means to treat the people.
SICINIUS. May they see his intent! He'll demand votes from them as if he despised what he was requesting them to give.
BRUTUS. Come, we'll inform them of our proceedings here. I know they're waiting for us in the marketplace.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 3 — Rome. The Forum
paragraphs: [Seven or eight Citizens enter.]
FIRST CITIZEN. Look, if he does ask for our votes, we shouldn't refuse him.
SECOND CITIZEN. We may refuse, sir, if we choose to.

THIRD CITIZEN. We have the power in ourselves to do it, but it's a power we have no right to use. For if he shows us his wounds and tells us his deeds, we're supposed to put our tongues into those wounds and speak for them. So if he tells us his noble deeds, we must also tell him our noble acceptance of them. Ingratitude is monstrous, and for the multitude to be ungrateful would make a monster of the multitude — and since we are members of it, we'd make ourselves into monstrous members.
FIRST CITIZEN. And it wouldn't take much to make us look worse. Once, when we stood up about the grain shortage, he himself didn't hesitate to call us the many-headed multitude.

THIRD CITIZEN. We've been called that by many — not because some of our heads are brown, some black, some auburn, some bald, but because our wits are so differently coloured. And honestly, I think if all our wits were to fly out of one skull, they would fly east, west, north, south, and the only direction they'd all agree on at once would be every point of the compass.
SECOND CITIZEN. You think so? Which way do you suppose my wit would fly?
THIRD CITIZEN. No, your wit won't come out as quickly as another man's will — it's wedged tight in a blockhead. But if it were set free, it would, for sure, head south.
SECOND CITIZEN. Why that way?
THIRD CITIZEN. To lose itself in a fog, where after three-quarters of it had melted away with rotten dews, the fourth quarter would come back, for conscience's sake, to help you get a wife.
SECOND CITIZEN. You're never without your jokes. You may, you may.
THIRD CITIZEN. Are you all resolved to give your votes? But that doesn't matter — the majority carries it. I say, if he would lean towards the people, there was never a worthier man.
[Coriolanus enters in a gown of humility, with Menenius.]

Here he comes, and in the gown of humility. Watch his behaviour. We're not to stand all together, but to come by him where he stands — by ones, by twos, and by threes. He has to make his requests individually, so each one of us has the personal honour of giving him our own vote with our own tongue. So follow me, and I'll direct you how to walk past him.
ALL. Agreed, agreed.
[They exit.]
MENENIUS. Oh sir, you're not doing this right. Haven't you known the worthiest men to do it?

CORIOLANUS. What am I supposed to say? "I beg you, sir" — damn it! I cannot bring my tongue to such a pace. "Look, sir, my wounds! I got them in my country's service when some of your brethren roared and ran from the noise of our own drums."
MENENIUS. Oh me, the gods! You mustn't speak of that. You must ask them to think kindly of you.
CORIOLANUS. Think of me! Hang them! I wish they would forget me, the way they forget the virtues our priests preach at them.
MENENIUS. You'll spoil everything. I'll leave you. Please speak to them, I beg you, in a wholesome manner.
[Menenius exits.]
CORIOLANUS. Tell them to wash their faces and keep their teeth clean.
[Three of the Citizens enter.]
Well, here comes a pair. You know the reason, sirs, why I'm standing here.
THIRD CITIZEN. We do, sir. Tell us what brought you to it.
CORIOLANUS. My own merit.
SECOND CITIZEN. Your own merit?
CORIOLANUS. Yes, but not my own desire.
THIRD CITIZEN. What — not your own desire?
CORIOLANUS. No, sir. It was never my desire to trouble the poor with begging.
THIRD CITIZEN. You must consider that if we give you anything, we hope to gain by you.
CORIOLANUS. Well then, tell me, what's your price for the consulship?
FIRST CITIZEN. The price is to ask for it kindly.
CORIOLANUS. Kindly, sir, I beg you, let me have it. I have wounds to show you, which shall be for your eyes only. — Your good vote, sir. What do you say?
SECOND CITIZEN. You shall have it, worthy sir.
CORIOLANUS. A deal, sir. There — two worthy votes begged in all. I have your alms. Adieu.
THIRD CITIZEN. But this is somewhat odd.
SECOND CITIZEN. If it were to give again — but it's no matter.
[Two citizens exit.]
[Two other Citizens enter.]
CORIOLANUS. Please now, if it suits the tune of your votes that I should be consul, I have here the customary gown.
FOURTH CITIZEN. You have served your country nobly, and you have not served it nobly.
CORIOLANUS. Your riddle?
FOURTH CITIZEN. You have been a scourge to her enemies; you have been a rod to her friends. You have not, indeed, loved the common people.

CORIOLANUS. You should think me the more virtuous for not having been common in my affection. I will, sir, flatter my sworn brother, the people, to earn a dearer estimation from them — it's a quality they think gentle. And since their wisdom is rather to have my hat than my heart, I will practise the insinuating nod and bow to them most counterfeitly. That is, sir, I will counterfeit the bewitchment of some popular man and give it bountifully to those who want it. So, I beg you, let me be consul.
FIFTH CITIZEN. We hope to find you our friend, and so we give you our votes heartily.
FOURTH CITIZEN. You have received many wounds for your country.
CORIOLANUS. I won't confirm your knowledge by showing them. I will value your votes highly and so trouble you no further.
BOTH CITIZENS. The gods give you joy, sir, heartily.
[The citizens exit.]

CORIOLANUS. Most sweet votes! Better to die, better to starve, than to beg for the pay we've already earned. Why should I stand here in this wolfish toga to beg from Hob and Dick the needless votes they offer? Custom calls me to it. But should we do everything just because custom wills it? If so, the dust on ancient time would lie unswept, and mountainous error would be heaped too high for truth to see over. Rather than play the fool like this, let the high office and the honour go to one who would do it this way. I'm halfway through — the one part I've suffered, the other I'll get done.
[Three more Citizens enter.]

Here come more votes. Your votes! For your votes I have fought; kept watch for your votes; for your votes carry two dozen and more wounds. Eighteen battles I have seen and heard of; for your votes I have done many things, some less, some more. Your votes! Indeed, I would be consul.
SIXTH CITIZEN. He has acted nobly, and cannot go without any honest man's vote.
SEVENTH CITIZEN. So let him be consul. The gods give him joy, and make him a good friend to the people!
ALL THREE CITIZENS. Amen, amen. God save you, noble consul.
[The citizens exit.]
CORIOLANUS. Worthy votes!
[Menenius enters with Brutus and Sicinius.]
MENENIUS. You've stood your appointed time, and the Tribunes endow you with the people's voice. What remains is that, invested with the official marks, you go presently to meet the Senate.
CORIOLANUS. Is this done?
SICINIUS. The custom of request you have discharged. The people do admit you, and are summoned to meet shortly upon your approbation.
CORIOLANUS. Where? At the Senate House?
SICINIUS. There, Coriolanus.
CORIOLANUS. May I change these clothes?
SICINIUS. You may, sir.
CORIOLANUS. I'll do it at once and, once I'm myself again, head to the Senate House.
MENENIUS. I'll keep you company. — Will you come along?
BRUTUS. We stay here for the people.
SICINIUS. Fare you well.
[Coriolanus and Menenius exit.]
He has it now; and from his looks, I think it sits warm at his heart.
BRUTUS. With a proud heart he wore his humble clothes. Will you dismiss the people?
[The Plebeians enter.]
SICINIUS. Well now, my masters, have you chosen this man?
FIRST CITIZEN. He has our votes, sir.
BRUTUS. We pray the gods he may deserve your love.
SECOND CITIZEN. Amen, sir. In my poor unworthy opinion, he mocked us when he begged our votes.
THIRD CITIZEN. Certainly, he flouted us outright.
FIRST CITIZEN. No, that's just his way of speaking. He didn't mock us.
SECOND CITIZEN. Every one of us, except yourself, says he used us scornfully. He should have shown us his marks of merit — wounds received for his country.
SICINIUS. Why, so he did, I'm sure.
ALL. No, no. No man saw them.

THIRD CITIZEN. He said he had wounds, which he could show in private, and with his hat, waving it like this in scorn, "I would be consul," says he; "ancient custom won't permit me without your votes; your votes therefore." When we granted that, here was "I thank you for your votes. Thank you. Your most sweet votes! Now that you have given your votes, I have nothing further to do with you." Wasn't that mockery?
SICINIUS. Why, either you were too ignorant to see it, or, seeing it, were so childishly friendly as to yield your votes?

BRUTUS. Couldn't you have told him as you were instructed? When he had no power, but was a petty servant to the state, he was your enemy, ever speaking against your liberties and the charters that you hold in the body of the commonwealth; and now, arriving at a place of power and influence in the state, if he should still maliciously remain a fast enemy to the plebeians, your votes might be curses against yourselves. You should have said that, as his worthy deeds claimed no less than what he stood for, so his gracious nature would think kindly of you for your votes, and translate his malice towards you into love, standing as your friendly lord.

SICINIUS. To have said this, as you were forewarned, would have touched his spirit and tested his inclination. From him you would have plucked either his gracious promise — which you might, as cause required, have held him to — or else it would have galled his surly nature, which doesn't easily endure any article binding him to anything. So, putting him into a rage, you should have taken advantage of his anger and passed him over, unelected.

BRUTUS. Didn't you notice he solicited you in open contempt when he needed your love — and do you think his contempt won't be bruising to you once he has the power to crush? Why, did your bodies have no heart among them? Or did you have tongues only to cry out against the rule of judgment?
SICINIUS. Have you ever denied a suitor before, and now again given your sought-for voices to a man who didn't ask but mocked?
THIRD CITIZEN. He's not confirmed yet. We may still deny him.
SECOND CITIZEN. And will deny him. I'll have five hundred votes of that opinion.
FIRST CITIZEN. I'll have twice five hundred, and their friends to back them.

BRUTUS. Get yourselves out of here at once, and tell those friends they have chosen a consul that will take their liberties from them, and reduce their voice to no more than dogs that are as often beaten for barking as they are kept for the purpose.

SICINIUS. Let them assemble, and on a wiser judgment, all revoke your ignorant election. Press home his pride and his old hatred of you. Besides, don't forget with what contempt he wore the humble clothes, how in his suit he scorned you. But your love, thinking on his services, made you ignore his present bearing, which he most jeeringly, ungravely, fashioned after the deep hatred he bears you.
BRUTUS. Lay the fault on us, your tribunes — that we laboured, with no obstacle between, until you had to cast your election for him.

SICINIUS. Say you chose him more by our command than by your own true affections, and that your minds, preoccupied with what you must do rather than what you should, made you against the grain vote him consul. Lay the fault on us.

BRUTUS. Yes, don't spare us. Say we read you lectures: how young he was when he began to serve his country; how long he has continued; what stock he springs from — the noble house of the Martians, from which came that Ancus Martius, Numa's daughter's son, who, after the great Hostilius reigned here, was king; and of the same house Publius and Quintus, who brought our best water here by conduits; and Censorinus, who was so named — and nobly named so, twice being censor — was his great ancestor.

SICINIUS. One thus descended, who has besides worked well in his own person to be set high in place, we did commend to your remembrance. But you have found, weighing his present bearing against his past, that he is your fixed enemy — and so revoke your sudden approbation.
BRUTUS. Say you never would have done it — keep harping on that — except by our urging. And presently when you have drawn your number, go straight to the Capitol.
ALL. We will do so. Almost all repent of their election.
[The Plebeians exit.]

BRUTUS. Let them go on. This mutiny is better put in hazard now than waiting, beyond doubt, for a greater one. If, as is his nature, he flies into a rage at their refusal, both observe and seize the advantage of his anger.
SICINIUS. To the Capitol, come. We'll be there before the stream of the people, and this will seem, as in part it is, their own doing, which we have goaded onward.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 1 — Rome. A street
paragraphs: [Cornets. Coriolanus, Menenius, all the gentry, Cominius, Titus Lartius and other Senators enter.]
CORIOLANUS. So Tullus Aufidius had raised a new force?
LARTIUS. He had, my lord, and that was what caused our swifter settlement.
CORIOLANUS. So then the Volscians stand only as at first — ready, when the time prompts them, to march against us again.
COMINIUS. They are so worn down, lord consul, that we shall hardly in our lifetimes see their banners wave again.
CORIOLANUS. Did you see Aufidius?
LARTIUS. Under safe conduct he came to me, and cursed the Volscians for having so basely yielded the town. He has retired to Antium.
CORIOLANUS. Did he speak of me?
LARTIUS. He did, my lord.
CORIOLANUS. How? What did he say?

LARTIUS. How often he had met you sword to sword; that of all things upon the earth he hated your person most; that he would pawn his fortunes to hopeless restitution, so he might be called your conqueror.
CORIOLANUS. He lives at Antium?
LARTIUS. At Antium.
CORIOLANUS. I wish I had a reason to seek him there, to oppose his hatred fully. Welcome home.
[Sicinius and Brutus enter.]
Look — these are the tribunes of the people, the tongues of the common mouth. I despise them, for they swagger about in authority against all noble forbearance.
SICINIUS. Go no further.
CORIOLANUS. Ha? What is that?
BRUTUS. It will be dangerous to go on. No further.
CORIOLANUS. What is causing this change?
MENENIUS. The matter?
COMINIUS. Hasn't he passed both the nobles and the commons?
BRUTUS. Cominius, no.
CORIOLANUS. Have I had only children's votes?
FIRST SENATOR. Tribunes, make way. He shall go to the marketplace.
BRUTUS. The people are incensed against him.
SICINIUS. Stop, or all will fall into riot.

CORIOLANUS. Are these your herd? Must these have voices, that can give them now and immediately disclaim them? What are your offices? You being their mouths, why don't you rule their teeth? Haven't you set them on?
MENENIUS. Be calm, be calm.
CORIOLANUS. This is a deliberate thing, and grows by plot — to curb the will of the nobility. Endure it, and live with those who cannot rule and never will be ruled.

BRUTUS. Don't call it a plot. The people cry that you mocked them; and lately, when corn was given to them free, you grumbled, slandered those who pleaded for the people, called them time-servers, flatterers, enemies to nobility.
CORIOLANUS. Why, this was known before.
BRUTUS. Not to all of them.
CORIOLANUS. Have you informed them since?
BRUTUS. What? I inform them?
COMINIUS. You're likely to do that sort of business.
BRUTUS. Not unlikely, in either case, to better yours.
CORIOLANUS. Why then should I be consul? By those clouds, let me deserve as ill as you do, and make me your fellow tribune.

SICINIUS. You show too much of that for which the people are stirred up. If you will pass to where you are bound, you must inquire your way — which you are out of — with a gentler spirit, or never be so noble as a consul, nor yoke with him as tribune.
MENENIUS. Let's be calm.
COMINIUS. The people are deceived, set on. This trickery does not become Rome, nor has Coriolanus deserved this dishonoured obstruction, falsely placed in the plain path of his merit.
CORIOLANUS. You tell me about corn? This was my speech, and I will speak it again.
MENENIUS. Not now, not now.
FIRST SENATOR. Not in this heat, sir, now.

CORIOLANUS. Now, as I live, I will. My nobler friends, I beg their pardon. As for the changeable, foul-smelling many, let them regard me, since I do not flatter, and in that see themselves. I say again: in soothing them we nourish against our senate the weed of rebellion, insolence, sedition, which we ourselves have ploughed for, sown, and scattered by mingling them with us — the honoured number, who lack neither virtue nor power, except what they have given to beggars.
MENENIUS. Well, no more.
FIRST SENATOR. No more words, we beseech you.

CORIOLANUS. What? No more? As I have shed my blood for my country, fearing no outward force, so shall my lungs coin words till their decay against those measles which we disdain should infect us, yet sought the very way to catch them.
BRUTUS. You speak of the people as if you were a god to punish, not a man of their infirmity.
SICINIUS. It would be well if we let the people know it.
MENENIUS. What, what? His temper?
CORIOLANUS. Temper? Were I as patient as midnight sleep, by Jove, this would still be my mind.
SICINIUS. It is a mind that shall remain a poison where it is, and poison no further.
CORIOLANUS. "Shall remain"? Do you hear this Triton of the minnows? Note his absolute "shall"?
COMINIUS. It was from the rule book.

CORIOLANUS. "Shall"? O good but most unwise patricians — why, you grave but reckless senators, have you thus given the Hydra leave to choose an officer, who, with his peremptory "shall," being but the horn and noise of the monster's, doesn't lack the spirit to say he'll turn your current into a ditch and make your channel his? If he has power, then veil your ignorance; if none, then wake up from your dangerous leniency. If you are learned, don't act like common fools; if you are not, let them have cushions beside you. You are plebeians if they are senators; and they are no less, when, both your voices blended, the largest taste most palates theirs. They choose their magistrate — and such a one as he, who sets his "shall," his popular "shall," against a graver bench than ever frowned in Greece. By Jove himself, it makes the consuls base! And my soul aches to know, when two authorities are up, neither supreme, how soon confusion may enter between the gap of both and take one by the other.
COMINIUS. Well, on to the marketplace.
CORIOLANUS. Whoever gave that counsel to give out the grain from the storehouse for free, as was sometimes done in Greece —
MENENIUS. Well, well, no more of that.
CORIOLANUS. Though there the people had more absolute power, I say they nourished disobedience and fed the ruin of the state.
BRUTUS. Why should the people give one who speaks like this their voice?

CORIOLANUS. I'll give my reasons, worthier than their votes. They know the corn was not our recompense, being well assured they never did service for it. When pressed to the war, even when the very navel of the state was touched, they would not pass through the gates. This kind of service did not deserve corn for free. In the war itself, their mutinies and revolts — where they showed the most valour — spoke nothing for them. The accusations they have often made against the Senate, with no cause behind them, could never be the native source of our so frank donation. Well, what then? How shall this swarming multitude digest the Senate's courtesy? Let deeds express what their words will likely be: "We did request it; we are the larger number, and in true fear they gave us our demands." Thus we debase the nature of our seats and make the rabble call our cautions fears, which will in time break open the locks of the Senate and bring in the crows to peck at the eagles.
MENENIUS. Come, enough.
BRUTUS. Enough, and over-measure.

CORIOLANUS. No, hear more! May whatever can be sworn by, both divine and human, seal what I end with!
