This double sovereignty — where one part disdains with cause, the other insults without any reason, where gentry, title, wisdom cannot conclude anything except by the yea and no of general ignorance — it must omit real necessities and give way meanwhile to unstable triviality. With purpose so barred, it follows that nothing is done to purpose. Therefore, I beg you — you that will be less fearful than discreet, that love the fundamental part of state more than you doubt the change of it, that prefer a noble life to a long one, and wish to dose a body with dangerous medicine that's sure to die without it — at once pluck out the multitudinous tongue; don't let them lick the sweet which is their poison. Your dishonour mangles true judgment and deprives the state of that integrity which should belong to it, since it lacks the power to do the good it would because of the ill that controls it.
BRUTUS. He has said enough.
SICINIUS. He has spoken like a traitor, and shall answer as traitors do.

CORIOLANUS. You wretch — may disdain overwhelm you! What should the people do with these bald-pated tribunes, on whom, depending, their obedience fails toward the greater bench? In a rebellion, when what was not fitting but what had to be was law, then were they chosen. In a better hour, let what is fitting be said to be fitting, and throw their power in the dust.
BRUTUS. Manifest treason.
SICINIUS. This — a consul? No.
BRUTUS. The aediles, ho! Let him be arrested.
[An Aedile enters.]
SICINIUS. Go call the people;
[The Aedile exits.]
in whose name I myself arrest you as a treasonous innovator, an enemy to the public welfare. Obey, I order you, and follow to answer for it.
CORIOLANUS. Get away, old goat.
ALL PATRICIANS. We'll stand surety for him.
COMINIUS.
[to Sicinius.] Aged sir, hands off.
CORIOLANUS.
[to Sicinius.] Get away, rotten thing, or I shall shake your bones
out of your garments.
SICINIUS. Help, you citizens!
[A rabble of Plebeians enter with the Aediles.]
MENENIUS. On both sides — more respect!
SICINIUS. Here's the one who would take from you all your power.
BRUTUS. Seize him, aediles.
ALL PLEBEIANS. Down with him, down with him!
SECOND SENATOR. Weapons, weapons, weapons!
[They all bustle about Coriolanus.]
Tribunes, patricians, citizens — what, ho! Sicinius, Brutus, Coriolanus, citizens!
ALL. Peace, peace, peace! Stay, hold, peace!
MENENIUS. What is about to happen? I am out of breath. Confusion is near. I cannot speak. You tribunes — to the people! — Coriolanus, patience! — Speak, good Sicinius.
SICINIUS. Hear me, people! Peace!
ALL PLEBEIANS. Let's hear our tribune. Peace! Speak, speak, speak.
SICINIUS. You are about to lose your liberties. Martius would have everything from you — Martius, whom lately you named for consul.
MENENIUS. Fie, fie, fie! This is the way to kindle, not to quench.
FIRST SENATOR. To tear down the city and lay all flat.
SICINIUS. What is the city but the people?
ALL PLEBEIANS. True — the people are the city.
BRUTUS. By the consent of all, we were established as the people's magistrates.
ALL PLEBEIANS. You so remain.
MENENIUS. And so are likely to do.
COMINIUS. That is the way to lay the city flat — to bring the roof down to the foundation and bury all that still distinctly stands in heaps and piles of ruin.
SICINIUS. This deserves death.
BRUTUS. Either let us stand by our authority or let us lose it. We do here pronounce, on behalf of the people, in whose power we were elected as theirs, that Martius is worthy of immediate death.
SICINIUS. Therefore lay hold of him, take him to the Tarpeian rock, and from there cast him into destruction.
BRUTUS. Aediles, seize him!
ALL PLEBEIANS. Yield, Martius, yield!
MENENIUS. Hear me one word. I beg you, tribunes, hear me but a word.
AEDILES. Peace, peace!
MENENIUS. Be what you seem — truly your country's friends — and proceed temperately to what you would so violently redress.
BRUTUS. Sir, those cold ways, which seem like prudent help, are very poisonous where the disease is violent. — Lay hands on him, and take him to the rock.
[Coriolanus draws his sword.]
CORIOLANUS. No; I'll die here. There are some among you who have seen me fighting. Come, try on yourselves what you have seen me do.
MENENIUS. Down with that sword! — Tribunes, withdraw for a while.
BRUTUS. Lay hands on him!
MENENIUS. Help Martius, help! You that are noble, help him, young and old!
ALL PLEBEIANS. Down with him, down with him!
[In this mutiny the Tribunes, the Aediles and the People are beaten back.]
MENENIUS. Go, get to your house. Begone, away. Otherwise all will come to nothing.
SECOND SENATOR. Get yourselves gone.
CORIOLANUS. Stand fast! We have as many friends as enemies.
MENENIUS. Shall it come to that?
FIRST SENATOR. The gods forbid! I beg you, noble friend, home to your house; leave us to cure this cause.
MENENIUS. For it is a sore on us you cannot lance yourself. Begone, I beseech you.
COMINIUS. Come, sir, along with us.
CORIOLANUS. I wish they were barbarians, as they truly are — though littered in Rome — and not Romans, as they are not, though dropped in the porch of the Capitol.
MENENIUS. Begone! Don't put your worthy rage into your tongue. One time will owe another.
CORIOLANUS. On fair ground I could beat forty of them.
MENENIUS. I could myself take up a brace of the best of them — yes, the two tribunes.

COMINIUS. But now the odds are beyond counting, and manhood is called foolishness when it stands against a falling structure. Will you go, before the rabble returns — whose rage tears like dammed-up waters and bears down what they are used to bearing?
MENENIUS. Please, begone. I'll try whether my old wit is in demand with those that have but little. This must be patched with cloth of any colour.
COMINIUS. No, come away.
[Coriolanus and Cominius exit.]
PATRICIAN. This man has marred his fortune.

MENENIUS. His nature is too noble for the world. He would not flatter Neptune for his trident or Jove for his power to thunder. His heart is his mouth; what his breast forges, that his tongue must vent — and, being angry, he forgets that he ever heard the name of death.
[A noise within.]
Here's fine work.
PATRICIAN. I wish they were in bed!
MENENIUS. I wish they were in the Tiber! What the vengeance — couldn't he speak to them fair?
[Brutus and Sicinius enter again with the rabble.]
SICINIUS. Where is this viper that would depopulate the city and be every man himself?
MENENIUS. You worthy tribunes —

SICINIUS. He shall be thrown down the Tarpeian rock with rigorous hands. He has resisted law, and therefore the law shall scorn him any further trial than the severity of the public power, which he so sets at nothing.
FIRST CITIZEN. He shall well know the noble tribunes are the people's mouths, and we their hands.
ALL PLEBEIANS. He shall, depend on it.
MENENIUS. Sir, sir —
SICINIUS. Peace!
MENENIUS. Don't cry havoc where you should only hunt with modest warrant.
SICINIUS. Sir, how is it that you have helped to make this rescue?
MENENIUS. Hear me speak. As I know the consul's worthiness, so can I name his faults.
SICINIUS. Consul? What consul?
MENENIUS. The consul Coriolanus.
BRUTUS. He — consul?
ALL PLEBEIANS. No, no, no, no, no!
MENENIUS. If, by the tribunes' leave and yours, good people, I may be heard, I would crave a word or two, which shall turn you to no further harm than the loss of so much time.

SICINIUS. Speak briefly then, for we are resolved to dispatch this viperous traitor. To eject him from here would be only one danger, and to keep him here our certain death. Therefore it is decreed: he dies tonight.
MENENIUS. Now the good gods forbid that our renowned Rome — whose gratitude towards her deserving children is enrolled in Jove's own book — should, like an unnatural dam, now eat up her own.
SICINIUS. He's a disease that must be cut away.

MENENIUS. O, he's a limb that has but a disease — mortal to cut off; easy to cure. What has he done to Rome that is worthy of death? Killing our enemies — the blood he has lost (which I dare vouch is more than what he has by many an ounce) — he shed for his country; and what is left, to lose it by his country would be to all of us who do it and suffer it a brand to the end of the world.
SICINIUS. This is utterly off course.
BRUTUS. Quite wrong. When he loved his country, it honoured him.
MENENIUS. The service of the foot, once gangrened, is not then respected for what it was before.
BRUTUS. We'll hear no more. Pursue him to his house and pluck him from there, lest his infection, being of a catching nature, spread further.

MENENIUS. One word more, one word! This tiger-footed rage, when it shall find the harm of unconsidered swiftness, will too late tie leaden weights to its heels. Proceed by due process, lest factions — for he is loved — break out and sack great Rome with Romans.
BRUTUS. If it were so —
SICINIUS. What are you talking about? Haven't we had a taste of his obedience? Our aediles struck! Ourselves resisted? Come.

MENENIUS. Consider this: he has been bred in the wars since he could draw a sword, and is poorly schooled in sifted language; flour and bran together he throws without distinction. Give me leave — I'll go to him and undertake to bring him where he shall answer in a lawful form, in peace, to his utmost peril.
FIRST SENATOR. Noble tribunes, it is the humane way: the other course will prove too bloody, and its end unknown from the beginning.
SICINIUS. Noble Menenius, be then as the people's officer. — Masters, lay down your weapons.
BRUTUS. Don't go home.
SICINIUS. Meet at the marketplace. We'll wait for you there. If you do not bring Martius, we'll proceed in our first way.
MENENIUS. I'll bring him to you.
[To Senators.] Let me ask for your company. He must come,
or what is worst will follow.
FIRST SENATOR. Please, let's go to him.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 2 — Rome. A room in Coriolanus’s house
paragraphs: [Coriolanus enters with Nobles.]

CORIOLANUS. Let them pull everything down about my ears, present me with death on the wheel or at wild horses' heels, or pile ten hills on the Tarpeian rock, so that the plunge would stretch down below the sight-line — yet I will still treat them like this.
FIRST PATRICIAN. You behave the nobler.

CORIOLANUS. I'm surprised my mother doesn't approve of me more, who used to call them woollen vassals, things created to buy and sell with pennies, to stand bare-headed in assemblies, to yawn, be still, and gape in wonder when anyone of my rank stood up to speak of peace or war.
[Volumnia enters.]
I'm speaking about you. Why did you wish me milder? Would you have me be false to my nature? Rather say I play the man I am.
VOLUMNIA. Oh, sir, sir, sir, I would have had you put on your power properly before you had worn it out.
CORIOLANUS. Let it go.

VOLUMNIA. You might have been quite the man you are with less striving to be so. The thwartings of your dispositions would have been less if you hadn't shown them how you were disposed before they lacked the power to cross you.
CORIOLANUS. Let them hang!
VOLUMNIA. Yes, and burn too.
[Menenius enters with the Senators.]
MENENIUS. Come, come, you have been too rough, something too rough. You must return and mend it.
FIRST SENATOR. There's no remedy, unless, by not doing so, our good city splits down the middle and perishes.
VOLUMNIA. Please, take counsel. I have a heart no less apt to anger than yours, but yet a brain that leads my use of anger to better advantage.

MENENIUS. Well said, noble woman. Before he should stoop to the herd like this — but for the fact that the violent fit of the time demands it as medicine for the whole state — I would put my armour on, which I can hardly bear.
CORIOLANUS. What must I do?
MENENIUS. Return to the Tribunes.
CORIOLANUS. Well, what then? What then?
MENENIUS. Repent what you have spoken.
CORIOLANUS. For them? I cannot do it to the gods. Must I then do it to them?

VOLUMNIA. You are too absolute — though in that you can never be too noble, except when extremities speak. I have heard you say that honour and policy, like inseparable friends, grow together in war. Grant that, and tell me — in peace, what does each of them lose by the other, that they do not combine there?
CORIOLANUS. Tush, tush!
MENENIUS. A good question.

VOLUMNIA. If in your wars it is honour to seem what you are not — which for your best ends you adopt as your policy — how is it any less or worse that it should hold companionship in peace with honour as in war, since it stands in equal demand for both?
CORIOLANUS. Why do you press this?

VOLUMNIA. Because now it falls to you to speak to the people, not by your own instruction, nor by the matter your heart prompts you to, but with such words that are only rooted in your tongue — though only bastards and syllables that find no acceptance in your heart's truth. Now, this dishonours you no more than taking a town with gentle words, which otherwise would put you to your fortune and the hazard of much blood. I would dissemble with my nature where my fortunes and my friends at stake required that I should do so in honour. I am in this — your wife, your son, these senators, the nobles. And you will rather show our general louts how you can frown than spend a fawn on them for the inheritance of their love and the safeguard of what its lack might ruin.
MENENIUS. Noble lady! — Come, go with us; speak fair. You may salve this way — not what is dangerously present, but the loss of what is past.

VOLUMNIA. I beg you now, my son, go to them with this hat in your hand, and having stretched it out so far — here, be with them — your knee kissing the stones — for in such business action is eloquence, and the eyes of the ignorant are more learned than the ears — waving your head, which often, thus correcting your stout heart, now humble as the ripest mulberry that will not bear the handling. Or say to them you are their soldier and, having been bred in conflicts, do not have the soft way, which you do confess would be fit for you to use, as for them to claim, in asking for their good love; but you will frame yourself, forsooth, hereafter as theirs, so far as you have power and person.
MENENIUS. This but done even as she speaks, why, their hearts would be yours; for they hand out pardons, being asked, as freely as words to little purpose.
VOLUMNIA. Please now, go, and be guided; although I know you would rather follow your enemy into a fiery gulf than flatter him in a bower.
[Cominius enters.]
Here is Cominius.
COMINIUS. I have been at the marketplace; and, sir, it is fitting you make a strong party or defend yourself by calmness or by absence. Everything is in anger.
MENENIUS. Only fair speech.
COMINIUS. I think it will serve, if he can bring his spirit to it.
VOLUMNIA. He must, and will. — Please now, say you will, and set about it.

CORIOLANUS. Must I go show them my unbarbered head? Must I, with my base tongue, give to my noble heart a lie that it must bear? Well, I will do it. Yet, were there only this single piece of ground to lose — this mould of Martius — they should grind it to dust and throw it against the wind. To the marketplace! You have now put me to such a part as I shall never carry out to the life.
COMINIUS. Come, come, we'll prompt you.
VOLUMNIA. I beg you now, sweet son, as you have said my praises first made you a soldier, so, to have my praise for this, perform a part you have not done before.

CORIOLANUS. Well, I must do it. Away, my own disposition, and let some harlot's spirit possess me! Let my throat of war be turned — which sang in chorus with my drum — into a pipe small as a eunuch's or the virgin voice that lulls babies asleep! Let knaves' smiles take root in my cheeks, and schoolboys' tears fill the glasses of my sight! Let a beggar's tongue move through my lips, and my armed knees, which bowed only in my stirrup, bend like his who has received alms! I will not do it, lest I cease to honour my own truth and, by my body's action, teach my mind a most inherent baseness.

VOLUMNIA. At your choice, then. To have to beg of you is more my dishonour than yours of them. Let everything come to ruin. Let your mother sooner feel your pride than fear your dangerous stoutness, for I mock at death with as big a heart as you. Do as you please. Your valour was mine; you sucked it from me, but you owe your pride to yourself.

CORIOLANUS. Please, be content. Mother, I am going to the marketplace. Chide me no more. I'll play mountebank to their love, cheat their hearts out of them, and come home beloved by all the trades in Rome. Look, I am going. Commend me to my wife. I'll return consul, or never trust again to what my tongue can do in the way of flattery.
VOLUMNIA. Do as you will.
[Volumnia exits.]
COMINIUS. Away! The Tribunes are waiting for you. Arm yourself to answer mildly, for they are prepared with accusations, as I hear, stronger than have yet been laid on you.
CORIOLANUS. The word is "mildly." Please, let us go. Let them accuse me by their inventions; I will answer in my honour.
MENENIUS. Yes, but mildly.
CORIOLANUS. Well, mildly be it, then. Mildly.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 3 — Rome. The Forum
paragraphs: [Sicinius and Brutus enter.]

BRUTUS. On this point press the charge home — that he aims at tyrannical power. If he evades us there, hit him with his contempt for the people, and the fact that the spoil taken from the Antiates was never distributed.
[An Aedile enters.]
Well, will he come?
AEDILE. He's coming.
BRUTUS. Accompanied by whom?
AEDILE. By old Menenius, and the senators who always favoured him.
SICINIUS. Have you a list of all the votes we have secured, set down by the poll?
AEDILE. I have. It's ready.
SICINIUS. Have you arranged them by tribes?
AEDILE. I have.

SICINIUS. Assemble the people here at once; and when they hear me say "It shall be so, by the right and strength of the commons," let it be either for death, for fine, or banishment — then let them, if I say "Fine," cry "Fine"; if "Death," cry "Death" — insisting on the old prerogative and power in the truth of the cause.
AEDILE. I shall inform them.
BRUTUS. And when at that time they have begun to cry, don't let them cease, but with a confused din enforce the immediate execution of whatever we happen to sentence.
AEDILE. Very well.
SICINIUS. Make them strong and ready for this signal, when we happen to give it them.
BRUTUS. Go about it.
[The Aedile exits.]

Put him into a rage straight away. He has been used always to conquering and to having the better of any contradiction. Once chafed, he cannot be reined back to temperance; then he speaks what's in his heart — and what's there will, with our help, break his neck.
[Coriolanus, Menenius and Cominius enter with other Senators.]
SICINIUS. Well, here he comes.
MENENIUS. Calmly, I do beseech you.

CORIOLANUS. Yes, like an ostler that for the smallest coin will bear the abuse of "knave" by the volume. — May the honoured gods keep Rome in safety and the chairs of justice supplied with worthy men! Plant love among us! Throng our great temples with the shows of peace, and not our streets with war!
FIRST SENATOR. Amen, amen.
MENENIUS. A noble wish.
[The Aedile enters with the Plebeians.]
SICINIUS. Draw near, you people.
AEDILE. Listen to your tribunes. Attention! Peace, I say!
CORIOLANUS. First, hear me speak.
BOTH TRIBUNES. Well, say. — Peace, ho!
CORIOLANUS. Shall I be charged with no further than this present? Must all be decided here?
SICINIUS. I demand to know if you submit yourself to the people's votes, accept their officers, and are content to suffer lawful censure for such faults as shall be proved against you.
CORIOLANUS. I am content.
MENENIUS. There, citizens, he says he is content. Consider the warlike service he has done. Think on the wounds his body bears, which show like graves in a holy churchyard.
CORIOLANUS. Scratches from briars, scars to provoke laughter only.

MENENIUS. Consider further, that when he speaks not like a citizen, you find him speaking like a soldier. Do not take his rougher tones for malicious sounds — but, as I say, such as become a soldier rather than envy you.
COMINIUS. Well, well, no more.
CORIOLANUS. What is the matter, that having been passed for consul with full voice, I am so dishonoured that in this very hour you take it off again?
SICINIUS. Answer to us.
CORIOLANUS. Say then. It's true, I ought to.
SICINIUS. We charge you that you have contrived to take from Rome all properly established office and to wind yourself into a tyrannical power — for which you are a traitor to the people.
CORIOLANUS. What? Traitor?
MENENIUS. No, temperately! Your promise.

CORIOLANUS. Let the fires of the lowest hell enfold the people! Call me their traitor? You injurious tribune! If within your eyes sat twenty thousand deaths, in your hands clutched as many millions, in your lying tongue both numbers — I would say "You lie" to you, with a voice as free as I do pray the gods.
SICINIUS. Do you mark this, people?
ALL PLEBEIANS. To the rock, to the rock with him!

SICINIUS. Peace! We need not add new matter to his charge. What you have seen him do, and heard him speak — beating your officers, cursing yourselves, opposing laws with blows, and here defying those whose great power must try him — even this, so criminal and in such capital kind, deserves the most extreme death.
BRUTUS. But since he has served well for Rome —
CORIOLANUS. What do you prattle about service?
BRUTUS. I speak of what I know.
CORIOLANUS. You?
MENENIUS. Is this the promise you made your mother?
COMINIUS. Hear me, I beg you —

CORIOLANUS. I'll hear no further. Let them pronounce the steep Tarpeian death, vagabond exile, flaying, pent up to linger on but a grain a day — I would not buy their mercy at the price of one fair word, nor check my courage for whatever they can give, to have it by saying "Good morrow."

SICINIUS. For the fact that he has, as much as in him lies, from time to time, raged against the people, seeking means to pluck away their power; as now, at last, given hostile strokes — and that not in the presence of dreaded justice, but on the ministers that distribute it — in the name of the people and in the power of us, the Tribunes, we, from this very instant, banish him from our city, on peril of being hurled from off the Tarpeian rock, never more to enter our Roman gates. In the people's name, I say it shall be so.
ALL PLEBEIANS. It shall be so, it shall be so! Let him away! He's banished, and it shall be so.
COMINIUS. Hear me, my masters and my common friends —
SICINIUS. He's sentenced. No more hearing.

COMINIUS. Let me speak. I have been consul and can show on me her enemies' marks for Rome. I love my country's good with a respect more tender, more holy and profound, than my own life, my dear wife's worth, her womb's increase, and the treasure of my loins. Then if I would speak that —
SICINIUS. We know your drift. Speak what?
BRUTUS. There's no more to be said, but that he is banished as enemy to the people and his country. It shall be so.
ALL PLEBEIANS. It shall be so, it shall be so!

CORIOLANUS. You common cry of curs — whose breath I hate like the reek of rotten fens, whose loves I prize as the dead carcasses of unburied men that corrupt my air — I banish you! And here remain with your uncertainty; let every feeble rumour shake your hearts; let your enemies, with the nodding of their plumes, fan you into despair! Have the power still to banish your defenders, till at length your ignorance — which doesn't find out till it feels, making but a reservation of yourselves, still your own foes — delivers you, like most abased captives, to some nation that won you without blows! Despising the city for you, thus I turn my back. There is a world elsewhere.
[Coriolanus and Cominius exit with the other Senators.]
AEDILE. The people's enemy is gone, is gone.
ALL PLEBEIANS. Our enemy is banished; he is gone. Hoo, hoo!
[They all shout and throw up their caps.]
SICINIUS. Go see him out at the gates, and follow him, as he has followed you, with all spite. Give him the vexation he deserves. Let a guard escort us through the city.
ALL PLEBEIANS. Come, come, let's see him out at the gates! Come! The gods preserve our noble tribunes! Come.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 1 — Rome. Before a gate of the city
paragraphs: [Coriolanus, Volumnia, Virgilia, Menenius, Cominius enter with the young nobility of Rome.]

CORIOLANUS. Come, dry your tears. A brief farewell. The many-headed beast butts me away. Come, mother, where is your ancient courage? You used to say that extremities were the test of spirits; that common chances common men could bear; that when the sea was calm, all boats alike showed mastery in floating; that fortune's blows, when they struck home hardest, being gently wounded needed a noble cunning. You used to load me with precepts that would make invincible the heart that learned them by heart.
VIRGILIA. O heavens! O heavens!
CORIOLANUS. No, I beg you, woman —
VOLUMNIA. Now may the red pestilence strike all trades in Rome, and every occupation perish!

CORIOLANUS. What, what, what! I shall be loved when I am missed. No, mother, recover that spirit when you used to say that if you had been the wife of Hercules, you would have done six of his labours and saved your husband so much sweat. — Cominius, don't droop. Adieu. — Farewell, my wife, my mother. I'll do well yet. — You old and true Menenius, your tears are saltier than a younger man's, and poisonous to your eyes. — My one-time general, I have seen you stern, and you have often beheld heart-hardening spectacles. Tell these sad women that it's as foolish to wail over inevitable strokes as it is to laugh at them. — My mother, you know well that my hazards have always been your consolation, and — don't take it lightly — though I go alone, like a lonely dragon whose fen is more feared and talked of than seen, your son will either exceed the common or be caught by cautious baits and stratagems.
VOLUMNIA. My first-born son, where will you go? Take good Cominius with you for a while. Decide on some course, rather than wild exposure to every chance that starts up in your way before you.
VIRGILIA. O the gods!

COMINIUS. I'll follow you a month, plan with you where you shall rest, so that you may hear of us and we of you; so if time should bring forth a cause for your recall, we shall not have to send across the vast world to seek a single man and lose the advantage, which always cools in the absence of the one who needs it.

CORIOLANUS. Farewell. You have years upon you, and you are too full of the surfeits of war to go roaming with one who's still unbruised. Just bring me out at the gate. — Come, my sweet wife, my dearest mother, and my friends of noble quality. When I am outside, bid me farewell, and smile. Please, come. While I remain above the ground, you shall still hear from me, and never anything of me but what is like me formerly.
MENENIUS. That's spoken as worthily as any ear can hear. Come, let's not weep. If I could shake off but seven years from these old arms and legs, by the good gods, I'd go with you every step.
CORIOLANUS. Give me your hand. Come.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 2 — Rome. A street near the gate
paragraphs: [The two Tribunes, Sicinius and Brutus, enter with the Aedile.]
SICINIUS. Send them all home. He's gone, and we'll go no further. The nobility are vexed, who we see have sided in his behalf.
BRUTUS. Now we have shown our power, let us seem humbler after it is done than when it was being done.
SICINIUS. Send them home. Say their great enemy is gone, and they stand in their ancient strength.
BRUTUS. Dismiss them home.
[The Aedile exits.]
Here comes his mother.
[Volumnia, Virgilia and Menenius enter.]
SICINIUS. Let's not meet her.
BRUTUS. Why?
SICINIUS. They say she's mad.
BRUTUS. They have taken note of us. Keep on your way.
VOLUMNIA. Oh, well met. May the hoarded plagues of the gods repay your love!
MENENIUS. Peace, peace! Don't be so loud.
VOLUMNIA. If only I could speak for weeping, you would hear — no, and you shall hear some. [To Sicinius.] Will you be gone?
VIRGILIA.
[To Brutus.] You shall stay too. I wish I had the power
to say so to my husband.
SICINIUS. Are you a man?
VOLUMNIA. Yes, fool — is that a shame? Just note this, fool: wasn't a man my father? Did you have the cunning of a fox to banish one who struck more blows for Rome than you have spoken words?
SICINIUS. O blessed heavens!

VOLUMNIA. More noble blows than you ever spoke wise words, and for Rome's good. I'll tell you what — yet go. No, but you shall stay too. I wish my son were in Arabia and your tribe before him, his good sword in his hand.
SICINIUS. What then?
VIRGILIA. What then? He'd make an end of your posterity.
VOLUMNIA. Bastards and all. Good man, the wounds he bears for Rome!
MENENIUS. Come, come, peace.
SICINIUS. I wish he had continued serving his country as he began, and not unknit the noble knot he had made.
BRUTUS. I wish he had.
VOLUMNIA. "I wish he had"? It was you who incensed the rabble. Cats — that can judge his worth as fittingly as I can judge those mysteries which heaven will not have Earth to know.
BRUTUS. Please, let's go.

VOLUMNIA. Now, please, sir, get yourself gone. You have done a brave deed. Before you go, hear this: as far as the Capitol exceeds the meanest house in Rome, so far does my son — this lady's husband here, this man, do you see? — whom you have banished, exceed all of you.
BRUTUS. Well, well, we'll leave you.
SICINIUS. Why do we stay to be baited by one who lacks her wits?
[The Tribunes exit.]
VOLUMNIA. Take my prayers with you. I wish the gods had nothing else to do but to confirm my curses. If I could meet them but once a day, it would unclog my heart of what lies heavy on it.
MENENIUS. You have told them off properly, and, on my word, you have cause. Will you sup with me?
VOLUMNIA. Anger is my meat. I sup upon myself, and so shall starve with feeding. Come, let's go. Leave off this faint whimpering, and lament as I do — in anger, like Juno. Come, come, come.
[They exit.]
MENENIUS. Fie, fie, fie!
[Menenius exits.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 3 — A highway between Rome and Antium
paragraphs: [A Roman and a Volscian enter.]
ROMAN. I know you well, sir, and you know me. Your name, I think, is Adrian.
VOLSCIAN. That's right, sir. Truly, I have forgotten you.
ROMAN. I am a Roman, and my services, like yours, are against them. Do you know me yet?
VOLSCIAN. Nicanor — no?
ROMAN. The same, sir.

VOLSCIAN. You had more beard when I last saw you, but your face is well confirmed by your voice. What's the news in Rome? I have a note from the Volscian state to seek you out there. You have nicely saved me a day's journey.
ROMAN. There have been in Rome strange insurrections — the people against the senators, patricians, and nobles.
VOLSCIAN. Have been? Is it over, then? Our state doesn't think so. They are in the most warlike preparation and hope to fall upon them in the heat of their division.

ROMAN. The main blaze of it is past, but a small thing would make it flare up again; for the nobles take the banishment of that worthy Coriolanus so to heart that they are in a ripe readiness to take all power from the people and to pluck their tribunes from them forever. This lies glowing, I can tell you, and is almost ripe for a violent outbreak.
VOLSCIAN. Coriolanus banished?
ROMAN. Banished, sir.
VOLSCIAN. You will be welcome with this news, Nicanor.

ROMAN. The day serves them well now. I have heard it said that the fittest time to corrupt a man's wife is when she has fallen out with her husband. Your noble Tullus Aufidius will show up well in these wars, his great opponent Coriolanus being now out of favour with his country.
VOLSCIAN. He cannot fail to. I am most fortunate to encounter you thus by chance. You have settled my business, and I will merrily accompany you home.
ROMAN. Between now and supper I shall tell you the strangest things from Rome, all tending to the good of their adversaries. Do you have an army ready, you say?
VOLSCIAN. A most royal one. The centurions and their charges, distinctly billeted, already on pay, and ready to be on foot at an hour's warning.
ROMAN. I am glad to hear of their readiness, and I am the man, I think, that shall set them in immediate action. So, sir, heartily well met, and most glad of your company.
VOLSCIAN. You take my words from me, sir. I have the most cause to be glad of yours.
ROMAN. Well, let us go together.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 4 — Antium. Before Aufidius’s house
paragraphs: [Coriolanus enters in mean apparel, disguised and muffled.]

CORIOLANUS. A goodly city is this Antium. City, it is I who made your widows. Many an heir of these fair buildings I have heard groan and drop before my wars. So don't recognize me, or your wives with spits and boys with stones will slay me in a puny battle.
[A Citizen enters.]
Save you, sir.
CITIZEN. And you.
CORIOLANUS. Direct me, if you will, where great Aufidius lives. Is he in Antium?
CITIZEN. He is, and is feasting the nobles of the state at his house tonight.
CORIOLANUS. Which is his house, please?
CITIZEN. This one here before you.
CORIOLANUS. Thank you, sir. Farewell.
[The Citizen exits.]

O world, your slippery turns! Friends now fast sworn, whose double bosoms seem to wear one heart, whose hours, whose bed, whose meal and exercise are always together, who twin, as it were, in inseparable love, shall within this hour, on a quarrel about a trifle, break out into the bitterest enmity; so the deadliest foes, whose passions and whose plots have broken their sleep to take one another, by some chance, some trick not worth an egg, shall grow dear friends and intermarry their children. So it is with me: I hate my birthplace, and my love is upon this enemy town. I'll go in. If he kills me, he does fair justice; if he gives me passage, I'll do his country service.
[He exits.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 5 — Antium. A hall in Aufidius’s house
paragraphs: [Music plays. A Servingman enters.]
FIRST SERVINGMAN. Wine, wine, wine! What service is this? I think our fellows are asleep.
[He exits.]
[Another Servingman enters.]
SECOND SERVINGMAN. Where's Cotus? My master calls for him. Cotus!
[He exits.]
[Coriolanus enters.]
CORIOLANUS. A handsome house. The feast smells good, but I don't look like a guest.
[The First Servingman enters.]
FIRST SERVINGMAN. What do you want, friend? Where are you from? There's no place for you here. Please, go to the door.
[He exits.]
CORIOLANUS. I have deserved no better welcome for being Coriolanus.
[The Second Servingman enters.]
SECOND SERVINGMAN. Where are you from, sir? — Has the porter got eyes in his head, that he gives entry to such company? — Please, get yourself out.
CORIOLANUS. Away!
SECOND SERVINGMAN. Away? Get yourself away.
CORIOLANUS. Now you are troublesome.
SECOND SERVINGMAN. Are you so brave? I'll have a word said to you soon.
[The Third Servingman enters; the First, coming in, meets him.]
THIRD SERVINGMAN. What fellow is this?
FIRST SERVINGMAN. A stranger one than I have ever looked on. I cannot get him out of the house. Please, call my master to him.
THIRD SERVINGMAN. What have you to do here, fellow? Please, get out of the house.
CORIOLANUS. Let me just stand. I'll not harm your hearth.
THIRD SERVINGMAN. What are you?
CORIOLANUS. A gentleman.
THIRD SERVINGMAN. A marvellously poor one.
CORIOLANUS. True, so I am.
THIRD SERVINGMAN. Please, poor gentleman, take up some other station. There's no place for you here. Please, get out. Come on.
CORIOLANUS. Get on with your job, go, and fatten on cold scraps.
[He pushes him away.]
THIRD SERVINGMAN. What — you won't? — Please, tell my master what a strange guest he has here.
SECOND SERVINGMAN. And I shall.
[He exits.]
THIRD SERVINGMAN. Where do you live?
CORIOLANUS. Under the canopy.
THIRD SERVINGMAN. Under the canopy?
CORIOLANUS. Yes.
THIRD SERVINGMAN. Where's that?
CORIOLANUS. In the city of kites and crows.
THIRD SERVINGMAN. In the city of kites and crows? What an ass he is! Then you live with jackdaws too?
CORIOLANUS. No, I don't serve your master.
THIRD SERVINGMAN. What, sir? You're meddling with my master?
CORIOLANUS. Yes — it's an honester service than meddling with your mistress. You prattle and prattle. Serve with your tray — get out!
[He beats him away.]
[The Third Servingman exits.]
[Aufidius enters with the Second Servingman.]
AUFIDIUS. Where is this fellow?
SECOND SERVINGMAN. Here, sir. I'd have beaten him like a dog, except for disturbing the lords inside.
AUFIDIUS. Where do you come from? What do you want? Your name? Why don't you speak? Speak, man. What's your name?
CORIOLANUS.
[Removing his muffler.] If, Tullus,
you don't yet know me, and, seeing me, don't take me for the man I am, necessity commands me to name myself.
AUFIDIUS. What is your name?
CORIOLANUS. A name unmusical to the Volscians' ears, and harsh in sound to yours.
AUFIDIUS. Say, what is your name? You have a grim appearance, and your face bears a command in it. Though your rigging is torn, you show a noble vessel. What's your name?
CORIOLANUS. Prepare your brow to frown. Do you know me yet?
AUFIDIUS. I don't know you. Your name?

CORIOLANUS. My name is Caius Martius, who has done to you in particular, and to all the Volscians, great harm and mischief — to which my surname Coriolanus may bear witness. The painful service, the extreme dangers, and the drops of blood shed for my thankless country are repaid only by that surname — a good memorial and witness of the malice and displeasure you should bear me. Only that name remains. The cruelty and envy of the people, permitted by our cowardly nobles — who have all forsaken me — have devoured the rest, and suffered me to be whooped out of Rome by the voice of slaves. Now this extremity has brought me to your hearth, not out of any hope — don't mistake me — to save my life; for if I had feared death, of all the men in the world I would have avoided you. But out of pure spite, to be fully even with those who banished me, I stand here before you. Then, if you have a heart for vengeance in you, that will revenge your own particular wrongs and stop those wounds of shame your country has suffered, hasten at once and make my misery serve your turn. Use it in such a way that my vengeful services may prove benefits to you, for I will fight against my cankered country with the spleen of all the under-fiends. But if you dare not do this, and that you are tired of trying further fortunes, then, in a word, I too am most weary of living any longer, and present my throat to you and to your ancient malice — which, not to cut, would show you only a fool, since I have ever pursued you with hate, drawn casks of blood out of your country's breast, and cannot live except to your shame, unless it be to do you service.

AUFIDIUS. O Martius, Martius, each word you have spoken has weeded a root of ancient envy from my heart. If Jupiter should from yonder cloud speak divine things and say it is true, I would not believe them more than you, all-noble Martius. Let me twine my arms about that body, against which my grained ash has broken a hundred times and scarred the moon with its splinters. Here I clip the anvil of my sword, and contest as hotly and as nobly with your love as ever in ambitious strength I contended against your valour. Know this first: I loved the maid I married; no man ever sighed truer breath. But seeing you here, you noble thing, my rapt heart dances more than when I first saw my wedded mistress step over my threshold. Why, you Mars, I tell you we have a force on foot, and I had purposed once more to hew your shield from your shoulder, or lose my arm for it. You have beaten me out twelve separate times, and I have nightly since dreamed of encounters between you and me; we have been down together in my sleep, unbuckling helmets, fisting each other's throats, and waked half dead with nothing. Worthy Martius, had we no other quarrel with Rome but that you are banished from there, we would muster all from twelve to seventy and, pouring war into the bowels of ungrateful Rome, like a bold flood overbear it. O, come, go in, and take our friendly senators by the hands, who now are here, taking their leave of me — for I am prepared to march against your territories, though not against Rome itself.
CORIOLANUS. You bless me, gods!

AUFIDIUS. Therefore, most absolute sir, if you will have the leading of your own revenges, take one half of my commission, and set down — as you are best experienced, since you know your country's strength and weakness — your own ways: whether to knock against the gates of Rome, or rudely visit them in remote parts, to frighten before destroying. But come in. Let me commend you first to those who shall say yes to your desires. A thousand welcomes! And more a friend than ever you were an enemy — yet, Martius, even that was much. Your hand. Most welcome!
[Coriolanus and Aufidius exit.]
[Two of the Servingmen come forward.]
FIRST SERVINGMAN. Here's a strange change!
SECOND SERVINGMAN. By my hand, I had thought to strike him with a cudgel, and yet my mind told me his clothes made a false report of him.
FIRST SERVINGMAN. What an arm he has! He turned me about with his finger and his thumb as one would set up a spinning top.
SECOND SERVINGMAN. No, I knew by his face there was something in him. He had, sir, a kind of face, I thought — I cannot tell how to describe it.
FIRST SERVINGMAN. He had so — looking as if — I'll be hanged, but I thought there was more in him than I could think.
SECOND SERVINGMAN. So did I, I'll be sworn. He is simply the rarest man in the world.
FIRST SERVINGMAN. I think he is. But you know a greater soldier than he is.
SECOND SERVINGMAN. Who — my master?
FIRST SERVINGMAN. No, it doesn't matter who.
SECOND SERVINGMAN. Worth six of him.
FIRST SERVINGMAN. No, not so either. But I take him to be the greater soldier.
SECOND SERVINGMAN. Honestly, look you, one cannot tell how to say that. For the defence of a town our general is excellent.
FIRST SERVINGMAN. Yes, and for an assault too.
[The Third Servingman enters.]
THIRD SERVINGMAN. O slaves, I can tell you news, news, you rascals!
FIRST and SECOND SERVINGMAN. What, what, what? Let's share it.
THIRD SERVINGMAN. I wouldn't be a Roman, of all nations; I'd just as soon be a condemned man.
FIRST and SECOND SERVINGMAN. Why? Why?
THIRD SERVINGMAN. Why, here's the man who used to thrash our general, Caius Martius.
FIRST SERVINGMAN. Why do you say, "thrash our general"?
THIRD SERVINGMAN. I don't say "thrash our general," but he was always good enough for him.
SECOND SERVINGMAN. Come, we're fellows and friends. He was ever too tough for him; I have heard him say so himself.
FIRST SERVINGMAN. He was too tough for him outright, to tell the truth of it, before Corioles; he hacked him and notched him like a piece of carbonado.
SECOND SERVINGMAN. And if he had been cannibal-minded, he might have boiled and eaten him too.
FIRST SERVINGMAN. But — more of your news?

THIRD SERVINGMAN. Why, he is so made over inside here as if he were son and heir to Mars; seated at the upper end of the table; no question is asked him by any of the senators but they stand bare-headed before him. Our general himself makes a darling of him, sanctifies himself with his hand, and rolls the whites of his eyes at his speech. But the bottom of the news is: our general is cut in half, and is only half of what he was yesterday — for the other has half, by the entreaty and grant of the whole table. He'll go, he says, and grab the porter of Rome's gates by the ears. He will mow all down before him and leave his passage stripped bare.
SECOND SERVINGMAN. And he's as likely to do it as any man I can imagine.

THIRD SERVINGMAN. Do it? He will do it! For look you, sir, he has as many friends as enemies — which friends, sir, as it were, did not, look you, sir, dare to show themselves, as we put it, his friends while he was in directitude.
FIRST SERVINGMAN. Directitude? What's that?
THIRD SERVINGMAN. But when they shall see, sir, his crest up again, and the man in blood, they'll come out of their burrows like rabbits after rain, and revel all with him.
FIRST SERVINGMAN. But when does this go forward?
THIRD SERVINGMAN. Tomorrow, today, presently. You'll have the drum struck up this afternoon. It's as it were part of their feast, and to be carried out before they wipe their lips.
SECOND SERVINGMAN. Why then, we shall have a lively world again. This peace is nothing but a way to rust iron, increase tailors, and breed ballad-makers.

FIRST SERVINGMAN. Give me war, I say. It exceeds peace as far as day does night. It's sprightly walking, audible, and full of vent. Peace is a very apoplexy, lethargy — mulled, deaf, sleepy, insensible; a maker of more bastard children than war is a destroyer of men.
SECOND SERVINGMAN. It's so, and as war in some sort may be said to be a ravisher, so it cannot be denied but peace is a great maker of cuckolds.
FIRST SERVINGMAN. Yes, and it makes men hate one another.
THIRD SERVINGMAN. The reason: because they then have less need of one another. The wars for my money! I hope to see Romans as cheap as Volscians. They are rising; they are rising.
ALL. In, in, in, in!
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 6 — Rome. A public place
paragraphs: [The two Tribunes, Sicinius and Brutus, enter.]

SICINIUS. We hear nothing of him, nor need we fear him. His remedies are toothless — the present peace, and the calm of the people, which before were in wild commotion. Here we make his friends blush that the world goes well, who would rather, though they themselves suffered by it, behold quarrelsome crowds pestering the streets than see our tradesmen singing in their shops and going about their business in a friendly way.
BRUTUS. We stood firm at the right time.
[Menenius enters.]
Is this Menenius?
SICINIUS. It is he, it is he. O, he has grown most kind of late. — Hail, sir!
MENENIUS. Hail to you both.
SICINIUS. Your Coriolanus is not much missed, except by his friends. The commonwealth stands, and would do so even were he more angry at it.
MENENIUS. All's well, and might have been much better if he could have temporized.
SICINIUS. Where is he, do you hear?
MENENIUS. No, I hear nothing; his mother and his wife hear nothing from him.
[Three or four Citizens enter.]
ALL CITIZENS. The gods preserve you both!
SICINIUS. Good evening, our neighbours.
BRUTUS. Good evening to you all, good evening to you all.
FIRST CITIZEN. Ourselves, our wives, and children, on our knees, are bound to pray for you both.
SICINIUS. Live and thrive!
BRUTUS. Farewell, kind neighbours. We wished Coriolanus had loved you as we did.
CITIZENS. Now the gods keep you!
BOTH TRIBUNES. Farewell, farewell.
[The Citizens exit.]
SICINIUS. This is a happier and more becoming time than when these fellows ran about the streets crying confusion.
BRUTUS. Caius Martius was a worthy officer in the war, but insolent, overcome with pride, ambitious, past all imagining self-loving.
SICINIUS. And aiming at one sole throne, without any partner.
MENENIUS. I don't think so.
SICINIUS. We should, by this point, to all our lamentation, if he had gone forth as consul, have found it so.
BRUTUS. The gods have well prevented it, and Rome sits safe and still without him.
[An Aedile enters.]

AEDILE. Worthy tribunes, there is a slave whom we have put in prison who reports that the Volscians, with two separate forces, have entered the Roman territories, and with the deepest malice of war destroy what lies before them.

MENENIUS. It's Aufidius, who, hearing of our Martius's banishment, thrusts forth his horns again into the world — horns that were shelled away when Martius stood for Rome, and dared not once peep out.
SICINIUS. Come, what are you talking about Martius for?
BRUTUS. Go see this rumour-monger whipped. It cannot be that the Volscians dare break with us.

MENENIUS. Cannot be? We have record that very well it can, and three examples of the same have happened within my lifetime. But reason with the fellow before you punish him, where he heard this, or you'll chance to whip your own intelligence and beat the messenger who tells you to beware of what should be dreaded.
SICINIUS. Don't tell me. I know this cannot be.
BRUTUS. Not possible.
[A Messenger enters.]
MESSENGER. The nobles in great earnestness are all going to the Senate House. Some news is coming that changes their countenances.
SICINIUS. It's this slave — go whip him in the people's sight — his raising, nothing but his report.
MESSENGER. Yes, worthy sir, the slave's report is seconded, and more, more fearful, is being delivered.
SICINIUS. What more fearful?

MESSENGER. It is spoken freely from many mouths — how probable, I do not know — that Martius, joined with Aufidius, leads a force against Rome and vows a revenge as wide as the span between the youngest thing and the oldest.
SICINIUS. This is most likely!
BRUTUS. Raised only so that the weaker sort may wish good Martius home again.
SICINIUS. The very trick of it.
MENENIUS. This is unlikely; he and Aufidius can no more reconcile than the most violent opposites.
[A Second Messenger enters.]

SECOND MESSENGER. You are sent for to the Senate. A fearful army, led by Caius Martius associated with Aufidius, rages upon our territories, and has already overborne their way, consumed with fire and taken whatever lay before them.
[Cominius enters.]
COMINIUS. O, you have made good work!
MENENIUS. What news? What news?
COMINIUS. You have helped to ravish your own daughters and to melt the city's leaden roofs upon your heads, to see your wives dishonoured before your noses —
MENENIUS. What's the news? What's the news?
COMINIUS. Your temples burned in their very cement, and your franchises, on which you stood, confined into an auger's bore.
MENENIUS. Please now, your news? — You have made fair work, I fear. — Please, your news? If Martius should be joined with the Volscians —

COMINIUS. If? He is their god; he leads them like a thing made by some other deity than Nature, that shapes man better; and they follow him against us brats with no less confidence than boys pursuing summer butterflies, or butchers killing flies.
MENENIUS. You have made good work, you and your apron-men, you that stood so much upon the voice of trades and the breath of garlic-eaters!
COMINIUS. He'll shake your Rome about your ears.
MENENIUS. As Hercules did shake down ripe fruit. You have made fair work.
BRUTUS. But is this true, sir?

COMINIUS. Yes, and you'll look pale before you find it otherwise. All the regions revolt smilingly, and whoever resists is mocked for valiant ignorance and perishes as a constant fool. Who is there that can blame him? Your enemies and his find something in him.
MENENIUS. We are all ruined, unless the noble man has mercy.

COMINIUS. Who shall ask for it? The tribunes cannot do it for shame; the people deserve such pity from him as the wolf does from the shepherds. As for his best friends, if they should say "Be good to Rome," they would charge him just as those should do who had deserved his hate, and in that showed themselves like enemies.

MENENIUS. It's true. If he were putting to my house the firebrand that should consume it, I haven't the face to say "I beseech you, cease." — You have made fine handiwork, you and your trades! You have crafted fine!
COMINIUS. You have brought such a trembling upon Rome as was never so incapable of help.
TRIBUNES. Don't say we brought it.
MENENIUS. What? Was it we? We loved him, but like beasts and cowardly nobles gave way to your clusters, who hooted him out of the city.

COMINIUS. But I fear they'll roar him in again. Tullus Aufidius, the second name among men, obeys his orders as if he were his officer. Desperation is all the policy, strength, and defence that Rome can make against them.
[A troop of Citizens enters.]

MENENIUS. Here come the clusters. — And is Aufidius with him? You are the ones who made the air unwholesome when you cast your stinking, greasy caps in hooting at Coriolanus's exile. Now he's coming, and not a hair on a soldier's head that won't prove a whip. As many coxcombs as you threw caps up he will tumble down, and pay you for your votes. It's no matter. If he could burn us all into one coal, we have deserved it.
ALL CITIZENS. Honestly, we hear fearful news.
FIRST CITIZEN. For my own part, when I said "banish him," I said it was a pity.
SECOND CITIZEN. And so did I.
THIRD CITIZEN. And so did I. And to tell the truth, so did very many of us. What we did, we did for the best; and though we willingly consented to his banishment, yet it was against our will.
COMINIUS. You are fine things, you voices!
MENENIUS. You have made good work, you and your shouting! — Shall we to the Capitol?
COMINIUS. O, yes, what else?
[Cominius and Menenius exit.]
SICINIUS. Go, masters, get yourselves home. Don't be dismayed. These are a side that would be glad to have this true, which they so seem to fear. Go home, and show no sign of fear.
FIRST CITIZEN. The gods be good to us! Come, masters, let's go home. I always said we were in the wrong when we banished him.
SECOND CITIZEN. So did we all. But, come, let's home.
[The Citizens exit.]
BRUTUS. I don't like this news.
SICINIUS. Nor I.
BRUTUS. Let's to the Capitol. I'd give half my wealth that this could be proved a lie!
SICINIUS. Please, let's go.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 7 — A camp at a short distance from Rome
paragraphs: [Aufidius enters with his Lieutenant.]
AUFIDIUS. Do they still flock to the Roman?

LIEUTENANT. I don't know what witchcraft is in him, but your soldiers use him as the grace before a meal, their talk at table, and their thanks at the end; and you are eclipsed in this campaign, sir, even by your own men.

AUFIDIUS. I cannot help it now, unless by taking action I cripple our whole design. He carries himself more proudly, even toward my person, than I thought he would when I first embraced him. Yet his nature is no changeling in that, and I must excuse what cannot be amended.
LIEUTENANT. Yet I wish, sir — I mean for your own sake — you had not joined commission with him, but either had carried out the campaign yourself or else left it to him alone.

AUFIDIUS. I understand you well, and be assured: when he shall come to his reckoning, he doesn't know what I can urge against him. Although it seems — and so he thinks, and it is no less apparent to the common eye — that he bears all things fairly, and shows good husbandry for the Volscian state, fights dragon-like, and conquers as soon as he draws his sword; yet he has left undone that which shall break his neck or hazard mine whenever we come to our reckoning.
LIEUTENANT. Sir, I beseech you, do you think he'll take Rome?

AUFIDIUS. All places yield to him before he even sits down outside them, and the nobility of Rome are his; the Senators and Patricians love him too. The Tribunes are no soldiers, and their people will be as rash in recalling him as they were hasty in expelling him from there. I think he'll be to Rome as the osprey is to the fish, who takes it by sovereignty of nature. At first, he was a noble servant to them, but he could not bear his honours level. Whether it was pride, which from daily good fortune always taints the lucky man; whether defect of judgment, in failing to dispose of those chances of which he was lord; or whether nature, unable to be anything other than one thing, not moving from helmet to cushion, but commanding peace with the same austerity and bearing with which he controlled war — one of these (since he has touches of all of them, but not all of them, for I dare go so far as to absolve him) made him feared, so hated, and so banished. But he has a merit that chokes complaint in the utterance. So our virtues lie in the interpretation of the time; and power, most commendable to itself, has no tomb so obvious as a chair to extol what it has done. One fire drives out one fire, one nail one nail; rights falter by rights, strengths fail by strengths. Come, let's away. When, Caius, Rome is yours, you are poorest of all; then shortly are you mine.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 1 — Rome. A public place
paragraphs: [Menenius, Cominius, Sicinius, Brutus (the two Tribunes), and others enter.]

MENENIUS. No, I'll not go. You hear what he has said to one who was once his general, who loved him most dearly. He called me father, but what of that? Go, you who banished him; a mile in front of his tent, fall down, and crawl on your knees the way into his mercy. No, if he was too coy to listen to Cominius speak, I'll stay home.
COMINIUS. He would not seem to know me.
MENENIUS. Do you hear?

COMINIUS. Yet at one moment he did call me by my name. I urged our old acquaintance, and the drops we have bled together. To "Coriolanus" he would not answer, forbade all names. He was a kind of nothing, titleless, until he had forged himself a name in the fire of burning Rome.
MENENIUS. Why, so; you have done good work! A pair of tribunes who have wrecked Rome to make coals cheap! A noble memory!
COMINIUS. I reminded him how royal it was to pardon when it was least expected. He replied that it was a bare petition from a state to one whom they had punished.
MENENIUS. Very well. Could he say less?

COMINIUS. I offered to awaken his concern for his private friends. His answer to me was that he could not stay to pick them out from a pile of foul, musty chaff. He said it was foolish for the sake of one poor grain or two to leave unburnt the heap and still keep smelling the offence.

MENENIUS. For one poor grain or two! I am one of those! His mother, wife, his child, and this brave fellow too — we are the grains; you are the musty chaff, and you are smelt above the moon. We must be burnt for you.

SICINIUS. No, please, be patient. If you refuse your aid in this so unprecedented need, yet do not reproach us with our distress. But surely, if you would be your country's pleader, your good tongue, more than the immediate army we can raise, might stop our countryman.
MENENIUS. No, I'll not meddle.
SICINIUS. Please, go to him.
MENENIUS. What should I do?
BRUTUS. Only test what your love for Rome can do toward Martius.
MENENIUS. Well, and say that Martius returns me, as Cominius was returned, unheard — what then? But as a discontented friend, grief-shot with his unkindness? Say it be so?
SICINIUS. Yet your good will must have that thanks from Rome in measure as you intended well.

MENENIUS. I'll undertake it. I think he'll hear me. Yet his biting his lip and humming impatiently at good Cominius much disheartens me. He wasn't caught at a good time; he hadn't dined. With the veins unfilled, our blood is cold, and then we sulk in the morning, are unfit to give or to forgive; but when we have stuffed these pipes and these conduits of our blood with wine and food, we have suppler souls than in our priestlike fasts. Therefore I'll watch him till he is fed for my request, and then I'll set upon him.
BRUTUS. You know the very road into his kindness, and cannot lose your way.
MENENIUS. Good faith, I'll try him, whatever the result. I shall before long have knowledge of my success.
[He exits.]
COMINIUS. He'll never hear him.
SICINIUS. Not?

COMINIUS. I tell you, he sits enthroned in gold, his eye red as if it would burn Rome; and his injury is the jailer to his pity. I kneeled before him; he very faintly said "Rise"; dismissed me with his silent hand. What he would do he sent after me in writing; what he would not do, bound with an oath that I yield to his conditions. So that all hope is vain unless his noble mother and his wife, who, as I hear, mean to petition him for mercy on his country. Therefore let's leave here and with our fair entreaties hurry them on.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 2 — An Advanced post of the Volscian camp before Rome
paragraphs: [Menenius enters and approaches the Watch, or Guard.]
FIRST WATCH. Stay! Where are you from?
SECOND WATCH. Stand, and go back.
MENENIUS. You guard like men; that's well. But by your leave, I am an officer of state, and I come to speak with Coriolanus.
FIRST WATCH. From where?
MENENIUS. From Rome.
FIRST WATCH. You may not pass; you must return. Our general will hear no more from there.
SECOND WATCH. You'll see your Rome embraced with fire before you'll speak with Coriolanus.
MENENIUS. Good my friends, if you have heard your general talk of Rome and of his friends there, the odds are my name has touched your ears. It is Menenius.
FIRST WATCH. Be that as it may; go back. The virtue of your name doesn't pass here.

MENENIUS. I tell you, fellow, your general is my dear friend. I have been the book of his good deeds, from which men have read his unparalleled fame happily amplified; for I have always vouched for my friends — of whom he is the chief — to the full size that truth could allow without lapsing. No, sometimes, like a bowl on a tricky surface, I have rolled past the throw, and in his praise have almost stamped a lie. Therefore, fellow, I must have leave to pass.

FIRST WATCH. Honestly, sir, if you had told as many lies on his behalf as you have spoken words on your own, you should not pass here — no, not though it were as virtuous to lie as to live chastely. Therefore, go back.
MENENIUS. Please, fellow, remember that my name is Menenius, always factionally on the side of your general.
SECOND WATCH. However you may have been his liar, as you say you have, I am one that, telling truth under him, must say you cannot pass. Therefore go back.
MENENIUS. Has he dined, can you tell? For I would not speak with him until after dinner.
FIRST WATCH. You are a Roman, aren't you?
MENENIUS. I am, as your general is.

FIRST WATCH. Then you should hate Rome as he does. Can you, when you have pushed out of your gates the very man who defends them, and, in violent popular ignorance, given your shield to your enemy, think to confront his revenges with the easy groans of old women, the virginal palms of your daughters, or with the palsied intercession of such a decayed old dotard as you seem to be? Can you think to blow out the intended fire your city is ready to flame in, with such weak breath as this? No, you are deceived. Therefore back to Rome and prepare for your execution. You are condemned. Our general has sworn you out of any reprieve or pardon.
MENENIUS. Sirrah, if your captain knew I were here, he would treat me with respect.
SECOND WATCH. Come, my captain doesn't know you.
MENENIUS. I mean your general.
FIRST WATCH. My general cares nothing for you. Back, I say, go, or I'll let out your half-pint of blood. Back! That's the most you'll have. Back!
MENENIUS. No, but fellow, fellow —
[Coriolanus enters with Aufidius.]
CORIOLANUS. What's the matter?

MENENIUS. Now, you companion, I'll say something on your behalf. You shall know now that I am held in respect; you shall see that a guardian Jack cannot keep me from my son Coriolanus. Just guess by my reception with him whether you don't stand in the state of being hanged or of some death longer in spectacle and crueller in suffering; behold it now, and swoon for what's coming upon you. [to Coriolanus.] May the glorious gods sit in hourly council about your particular prosperity and love you no less than your old father Menenius does! O my son, my son! You are preparing fire for us; look here — here is water to quench it. I was hardly moved to come to you; but being assured that none but I could move you, I have been blown out of your gates with sighs, and I conjure you to pardon Rome and your petitioning countrymen. The good gods assuage your wrath and turn the dregs of it upon this varlet here, this fellow, who, like a block, has denied my access to you.
CORIOLANUS. Away!
MENENIUS. What? Away?

CORIOLANUS. Wife, mother, child — I know them not. My affairs are servants to others. Though my revenge is properly my own, my remission lies in Volscian breasts. That we have been intimate friends — ungrateful forgetfulness shall poison rather than pity note how much. Therefore begone. My ears against your suits are stronger than your gates against my force. Yet, because I loved you, take this along; I wrote it for your sake,
[He gives Menenius a paper.]
and would have sent it. Not another word, Menenius — I will not hear you speak. — This man, Aufidius, was my beloved in Rome; yet you see how it is.
AUFIDIUS. You keep a constant temper.
[They exit.]
[The Guard and Menenius remain.]
FIRST WATCH. Now, sir, is your name Menenius?
SECOND WATCH. It's a spell, you see, of much power. You know the way home again.
FIRST WATCH. Do you hear how we are scolded for keeping Your Greatness back?
SECOND WATCH. What reason do you think I have to swoon?

MENENIUS. I care nothing for the world nor for your general. For such things as you, I can scarcely think there are any, you're so slight. He who has a will to die at his own hand does not fear it from another. Let your general do his worst. As for you, be what you are, long; and your misery increase with your age! I say to you, as I was said to, away!
[He exits.]
FIRST WATCH. A noble fellow, I'll warrant him.
SECOND WATCH. The worthy fellow is our general. He is the rock, the oak not to be shaken by the wind.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 3 — The tent of Coriolanus
paragraphs: [Coriolanus and Aufidius enter.]
CORIOLANUS. Tomorrow we will set down our army before the walls of Rome. My partner in this campaign, you must report to the Volscian lords how openly I have conducted this business.
AUFIDIUS. Only their ends have you respected, stopped your ears against the general appeal of Rome; never admitted a private whisper, no, not even from such friends as thought themselves sure of you.

CORIOLANUS. This last old man, whom with a cracked heart I have sent back to Rome, loved me beyond a father's measure — no, made a god of me, indeed. Their last refuge was to send him, for whose old love I have — though I behaved sourly to him — once more offered the original conditions, which they did refuse and cannot now accept, simply to oblige him who thought he could do more. To very little have I yielded. Fresh embassies and pleas, neither from the state nor from private friends, will I lend an ear to hereafter.
[Shout within.]
Ha? What shout is that? Shall I be tempted to break my vow at the very moment it's made? I will not.
[Virgilia, Volumnia, Valeria, young Martius enter with attendants.]

My wife comes first, then the honoured mould in which this trunk was framed, and in her hand the grandchild of her blood. But out, affection! Break, every bond and privilege of nature! Let it be virtuous to be obstinate. What is that curtsy worth? Or those doves' eyes, which can make gods forsworn? I melt, and am not of stronger earth than other men. My mother bows, as if Olympus to a molehill should bend in supplication; and my young boy has an aspect of intercession that great Nature cries out "Don't deny!" Let the Volscians plough Rome and harrow Italy — I'll never be such a gosling as to obey instinct, but stand as if a man were author of himself, and knew no other kin.
VIRGILIA. My lord and husband.
CORIOLANUS. These eyes are not the same I wore in Rome.
VIRGILIA. The sorrow that gives us back to you thus changed makes you think so.
CORIOLANUS. Like a dull actor now, I have forgotten my part, and I am out, to my full disgrace. Best of my flesh, forgive my tyranny, but do not therefore say, "Forgive our Romans."
[They kiss.]

O, a kiss long as my exile, sweet as my revenge! Now, by the jealous queen of heaven, that kiss I carried away from you, dear, and my true lip has kept it virgin ever since. You gods! I prattle, and the most noble mother of the world I leave unsaluted. Sink, my knee, into the earth;
[He kneels.]
show more impression of your deep duty than common sons do.
VOLUMNIA. O, stand up, blessed,
[He rises.]
while with no softer cushion than the flint I kneel before you, and improperly show duty, the relation between child and parent being all this while mistaken.
[She kneels.]
CORIOLANUS. What is this? Your knees to me? To your corrected son?
[He raises her up.]
Then let the pebbles on the hungry beach flick the stars! Then let the mutinous winds drive the proud cedars against the fiery sun, murdering impossibility to make what cannot be a light task.
VOLUMNIA. You are my warrior; I helped to frame you. Do you know this lady?
CORIOLANUS. The noble sister of Publicola, the moon of Rome, chaste as the icicle curdled by frost from the purest snow and hanging on Diana's temple! — Dear Valeria.
VOLUMNIA. This is a poor little version of yourself, who, with the interpretation of full time, may show like all of you.

CORIOLANUS. The god of soldiers, with the consent of supreme Jove, inform your thoughts with nobleness, so that you may prove invulnerable to shame, and stand in the wars like a great sea-mark, withstanding every gust and saving those who set eyes on you.
VOLUMNIA.
[To young Martius.] Your knee, sirrah.
[He kneels.]
CORIOLANUS. That's my brave boy!
VOLUMNIA. Even he, your wife, this lady, and myself are suitors to you.
[Young Martius rises.]

CORIOLANUS. I beseech you, peace; or, if you would ask, remember this beforehand: the thing I have sworn not to grant must not be considered by you as a denial. Do not bid me dismiss my soldiers or capitulate again with Rome's mechanics. Do not tell me in what I seem unnatural; do not desire to soothe my rages and revenges with your colder reasoning.

VOLUMNIA. O, no more, no more! You have said you will not grant us anything; for we have nothing else to ask but that which you have already denied. Yet we will ask, so that if you fail in our request, the blame may hang on your hardness. Therefore, hear us.
CORIOLANUS. Aufidius, and you Volscians, mark, for we'll hear nothing from Rome in private. Your request?

VOLUMNIA. Were we silent, and didn't speak, our clothing and the state of our bodies would betray what kind of life we have led since your exile. Think to yourself how, more unfortunate than all living women, we have come here. Your very sight, which should make our eyes flow with joy and hearts dance with comfort, instead makes them weep and shake with fear and sorrow, forcing the mother, wife, and child to see the son, the husband, and the father tearing out his country's bowels. And to poor us, your enmity is most fatal. You bar us our prayers to the gods, which is a comfort all but us enjoy. For how can we — alas, how can we — pray for our country, to which we are bound, together with your victory, to which we are bound? Alas, either we must lose our country, our dear nurse, or else your person, our comfort in the country. We must find an evident calamity, even if we had our wish — whichever side should win — for either you must be led like a foreign turncoat with manacles through our streets, or else triumphantly tread on your country's ruin, and bear the palm for having bravely shed your wife's and children's blood. For myself, son, I do not intend to wait on fortune till these wars decide themselves. If I cannot persuade you rather to show a noble grace to both sides than to seek the destruction of one, you shall no sooner march to assault your country than you shall tread — trust to it, you shall not — on your mother's womb that brought you into this world.
VIRGILIA. Yes, and mine, that brought you forth this boy to keep your name alive into time.
YOUNG MARTIUS. He shall not tread on me. I'll run away till I am bigger, but then I'll fight.
CORIOLANUS. Not to be possessed of a woman's tenderness requires the sight neither of child nor woman. — I have sat too long.
[He rises.]

VOLUMNIA. No, don't leave us like this. If it were the case that our request tended to save the Romans by destroying the Volscians whom you serve, you might condemn us as poisonous of your honour. No, our petition is that you reconcile them, so that the Volscians may say "This mercy we have shown," the Romans "This we received," and each, on either side, give the all-hail to you and cry, "Be blessed for making up this peace!" You know, great son, the outcome of war is uncertain — but this is certain: that, if you conquer Rome, the benefit you shall reap by it is such a name as will be dogged with curses whenever it is spoken, whose chronicle will be written thus: "The man was noble, but with his last attempt he wiped it out; destroyed his country, and his name remains to the following age abhorred." Speak to me, son. You have set yourself to imitate the fine strains of honour, the graces of the gods — to tear the wide cheeks of the air with thunder, and yet to charge your sulphur with a bolt that should only split an oak. Why don't you speak? Do you think it honourable for a noble man still to remember wrongs? — Daughter, you speak. He cares nothing for your weeping. — You speak, boy. Perhaps your childishness will move him more than our reasoning can. — There is no man in the world more bound to his mother — yet here he lets me prattle on like one in the stocks. You have never in your life shown your dear mother any courtesy, when she, poor hen, with no second brood to care for, has clucked you to the wars and safely home, loaded with honour. Say my request is unjust and spurn me back; but if it is not, you are not honest, and the gods will plague you for holding back from me the duty that belongs to a mother's role. — He turns away. — Down, ladies! Let us shame him with our knees. To his surname Coriolanus belongs more pride than pity for our prayers. Down! An end.
[They kneel.]

This is the last. So we will go home to Rome and die among our neighbours. — No, look at us. This boy that cannot tell what he would have, but kneels and holds up hands for fellowship, reasons our petition with more strength than you have to deny it. — Come, let us go.
[They rise.]

This fellow had a Volscian for his mother, his wife is in Corioles, and his child looks like him by chance. — Yet give us our answer. I am silent until our city is on fire, and then I'll speak a little.
[He holds her by the hand, silent.]

CORIOLANUS. O mother, mother! What have you done? Look — the heavens open, the gods look down, and this unnatural scene they laugh at. O my mother, mother, O! You have won a happy victory for Rome; but, for your son — believe it, O, believe it! — most dangerously you have prevailed with him, if not most fatally to him. But let it come. — Aufidius, though I cannot make true wars, I'll frame convenient peace. Now, good Aufidius, were you in my place, would you have heard a mother less? Or granted less, Aufidius?
AUFIDIUS. I was moved by it.

CORIOLANUS. I dare swear you were. And, sir, it is no small thing to make my eyes sweat compassion. But, good sir, what peace you intend to make, advise me. For my part, I'll not go to Rome — I'll back with you; and please, stand by me in this cause. — O mother! — Wife!
[He speaks with them aside.]
AUFIDIUS.
[Aside.] I'm glad you have set your mercy and your honour
at odds in yourself. Out of that, I'll work myself back to my former fortune.
CORIOLANUS.
[To the Women.] Yes, by and by;

but we'll drink together, and you shall bear back a better witness than words, which we, on similar conditions, will have countersealed. Come, enter with us. Ladies, you deserve to have a temple built to you. All the swords in Italy, and her allied forces, could not have made this peace.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 4 — Rome. A public place
paragraphs: [Menenius and Sicinius enter.]
MENENIUS. Do you see that corner of the Capitol, that cornerstone?
SICINIUS. Why, what of that?

MENENIUS. If it's possible for you to dislodge it with your little finger, there's some hope the ladies of Rome — especially his mother — may prevail with him. But I say there is no hope in it. Our throats are sentenced and only awaiting execution.
SICINIUS. Is it possible that so short a time can change the condition of a man?
MENENIUS. There is a difference between a grub and a butterfly, yet your butterfly was a grub. This Martius has grown from man to dragon. He has wings; he's more than a creeping thing.
SICINIUS. He loved his mother dearly.

MENENIUS. So did he me; and he remembers his mother no more now than an eight-year-old horse. The sourness of his face turns ripe grapes bitter. When he walks, he moves like an engine, and the ground shrinks before his tread. He is able to pierce a breastplate with his eye, talks like a death-bell, and his hum is an artillery battery. He sits enthroned as a thing made for Alexander. What he commands to be done is finished with his commanding. He lacks nothing of a god but eternity and a heaven to throne in.
SICINIUS. Yes, mercy — if you report him truly.

MENENIUS. I paint him exactly. Mark what mercy his mother shall bring out of him. There is no more mercy in him than there is milk in a male tiger. That our poor city shall find, and all of this is owing to you.
SICINIUS. May the gods be good to us.
MENENIUS. No, in such a case the gods will not be good to us. When we banished him, we did not respect them; and now he returns to break our necks, they don't respect us.
[A Messenger enters.]

MESSENGER. Sir, if you would save your life, fly to your house. The plebeians have caught your fellow tribune and drag him up and down, all swearing that if the Roman ladies bring no comfort home, they'll kill him inch by inch.
[Another Messenger enters.]
SICINIUS. What's the news?
SECOND MESSENGER. Good news, good news! The ladies have prevailed. The Volscians have struck camp, and Martius is gone. A merrier day never yet greeted Rome — no, not the expulsion of the Tarquins.
SICINIUS. Friend, are you certain this is true? Is it most certain?

SECOND MESSENGER. As certain as I know the sun is fire. Where have you been lurking, that you doubt it? Never did the blown tide hurry through an arch as the comforted citizens through the gates. Why, listen!
[Trumpets, hautboys, drums beat, all together.]
The trumpets, sackbuts, psalteries, and fifes, tabors and cymbals, and the shouting Romans make the sun dance. Listen!
[A shout within.]

MENENIUS. This is good news. I will go meet the ladies. This Volumnia is worth a city full of consuls, senators, patricians; of tribunes such as you, a whole sea and land full. You have prayed well today. This morning, for ten thousand of your throats I'd not have given a single coin. Listen, how they rejoice!
[Sound continues with the shouts.]
SICINIUS. First, the gods bless you for your tidings; next, accept my thankfulness.
SECOND MESSENGER. Sir, we have all great cause to give great thanks.
SICINIUS. They are near the city?
MESSENGER. Almost at the point of entering.
SICINIUS. We'll meet them, and help the joy.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 5 — Rome. A street near the gate
paragraphs: [Two Senators enter, with the Ladies (Volumnia, Virgilia, Valeria) passing over the stage, along with other Lords.]

SENATOR. Behold our patroness, the life of Rome! Call all your tribes together, praise the gods, and make triumphant fires. Strew flowers before them, unshout the noise that banished Martius, recall him with the welcome of his mother. Cry, "Welcome, ladies, welcome!"
ALL. Welcome, ladies, welcome!
[A flourish with drums and trumpets.]
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 6 — Antium. A public place
paragraphs: [Tullus Aufidius enters with Attendants.]
AUFIDIUS. Go tell the lords of the city I am here. Deliver them this paper.
[He gives them a paper.]
