Having read it, bid them go to the marketplace, where I, in their ears and in the commons' ears, will vouch the truth of it. The man I accuse, by this time, has entered the city gates and intends to appear before the people, hoping to clear himself with words. Hurry.
[The Attendants exit.]
[Three or four Conspirators of Aufidius's faction enter.]
Most welcome!
FIRST CONSPIRATOR. How is it with our general?
AUFIDIUS. Just as with a man poisoned by his own alms and slain by his own charity.
SECOND CONSPIRATOR. Most noble sir, if you still hold the same intent in which you wished us partners, we'll deliver you from your great danger.
AUFIDIUS. Sir, I cannot say. We must proceed as we find the people respond.
THIRD CONSPIRATOR. The people will remain uncertain while there's a difference between you, but the fall of either makes the survivor heir of all.

AUFIDIUS. I know it, and my pretext for striking at him admits a good construction. I raised him, and I pawned my honour for his truth — who, being so elevated, watered his new plants with the dews of flattery, seducing my friends in this way; and to this end he bent his nature, which had never before been known to be anything but rough, unswayable, and free.
THIRD CONSPIRATOR. Sir, his stoutness when he stood for consul, which he lost by lack of stooping —

AUFIDIUS. That's what I would have spoken of. Being banished for it, he came to my hearth, and presented his throat to my knife. I took him, made him joint partner with me, gave way to all his own desires; no, I let him choose, out of my ranks, my best and freshest men for his own projects to accomplish; served his designs in my own person; helped to reap the fame which he made all his own; and took a certain pride in doing myself this wrong, till at last I seemed his follower, not his partner; and he paid me with his condescending looks as if I had been a hired mercenary.
FIRST CONSPIRATOR. So he did, my lord. The army marvelled at it, and, in the end, when he had carried Rome and we looked for no less spoil than glory —

AUFIDIUS. There was the point on which my sinews shall be stretched against him. For a few drops of women's tears — which are as cheap as lies — he sold the blood and labour of our great campaign. Therefore he shall die, and I'll renew myself in his fall. But, listen!
[Drums and trumpets sound, with great shouts from the people.]
FIRST CONSPIRATOR. Your native town you entered like a messenger, with no welcome home; but he returns splitting the air with noise.
SECOND CONSPIRATOR. And patient fools, whose children he has slain, tear their base throats by giving him glory.

THIRD CONSPIRATOR. Therefore, at your opportunity, before he can express himself or move the people with what he would say, let him feel your sword — which we will second. When he lies stretched out, after your manner, his tale once pronounced shall bury his reasons along with his body.
AUFIDIUS. Say no more. Here come the lords.
[The Lords of the city enter.]
ALL LORDS. You are most welcome home.
AUFIDIUS. I have not deserved it. But, worthy lords, have you with care read what I have written to you?
ALL LORDS. We have.

FIRST LORD. And grieve to hear it. What faults he made before the last, I think, might have found easy fines, but to end there where he was to begin, and give away the benefit of our levies, paying us back with our own expense, making a treaty where a yielding was at hand — this admits no excuse.
[Coriolanus enters marching with Drum and Colours, the Commoners being with him.]
AUFIDIUS. He approaches. You shall hear him.

CORIOLANUS. Hail, lords! I am returned as your soldier, no more infected with my country's love than when I left here, but still subsisting under your great command. You are to know that I have prosperously attempted, and with bloody passage led your wars even to the gates of Rome. The spoils we have brought home more than counterbalance a full third part of the campaign's expenses. We have made peace with no less honour to the Antiates than shame to the Romans, and we here deliver, signed by the Consuls and Patricians, together with the seal of the Senate, what we have agreed to.
[He offers the lords a paper.]
AUFIDIUS. Do not read it, noble lords, but tell the traitor in the highest degree how he has abused your powers.
CORIOLANUS. "Traitor?" How now?
AUFIDIUS. Yes, traitor, Martius.
CORIOLANUS. Martius?

AUFIDIUS. Yes, Martius, Caius Martius. Do you think I'll grace you with that robbery, your stolen name Coriolanus, in Corioles? You lords and heads of state, perfidiously he has betrayed your interests and given up for certain drops of salt your city Rome — I say your city — to his wife and mother, breaking his oath and resolution like a twist of rotten silk, never admitting any counsel of war, but at his nurse's tears he whined and roared away your victory, so that pages blushed at him and men of heart looked, wondering, at each other.
CORIOLANUS. Do you hear, Mars?
AUFIDIUS. Don't name the god, you boy of tears.
CORIOLANUS. Ha?
AUFIDIUS. No more.

CORIOLANUS. Measureless liar, you have made my heart too great for what contains it. "Boy"? O slave! — Pardon me, lords, this is the first time I was ever forced to scold. Your judgments, my grave lords, must give this cur the lie; and his own knowledge — who wears my stripes impressed upon him, that must bear my beating to his grave — shall join to thrust the lie back upon him.
FIRST LORD. Peace, both, and hear me speak.

CORIOLANUS. Cut me to pieces, Volscians. Men and lads, stain all your blade-edges on me. "Boy"? False hound! If you have written your annals true, it is there that, like an eagle in a dovecote, I fluttered your Volscians in Corioles. Alone I did it. "Boy"!
AUFIDIUS. Why, noble lords, will you be reminded of his blind fortune — which was your shame — by this unholy braggart, before your own eyes and ears?
ALL CONSPIRATORS. Let him die for it.
ALL PEOPLE. Tear him to pieces! Do it presently! He killed my son! My daughter! He killed my cousin Marcus! He killed my father!

SECOND LORD. Peace, ho! No outrage! Peace! The man is noble, and his fame folds in this orb of the Earth. His last offences to us shall have judicious hearing. Stand back, Aufidius, and don't trouble the peace.
CORIOLANUS. O that I had him, with six Aufidiuses, or more of his tribe, to use my lawful sword.
AUFIDIUS. Insolent villain!
ALL CONSPIRATORS. Kill, kill, kill, kill, kill him!
[The Conspirators draw, and kill Martius, who falls. Aufidius stands on him.]
LORDS. Hold, hold, hold, hold!
AUFIDIUS. My noble masters, hear me speak.
FIRST LORD. O Tullus!
SECOND LORD. You have done a deed at which valour will weep.
THIRD LORD. Don't tread upon him. — Masters, all be quiet. — Put up your swords.

AUFIDIUS. My lords, when you shall know — as in this rage, provoked by him, you cannot — the great danger which this man's life owed you, you'll rejoice that he is thus cut off. May it please your Honours to call me to your senate, and I'll deliver myself as your loyal servant, or endure your heaviest censure.
FIRST LORD. Carry his body from here, and mourn for him. Let him be regarded as the most noble corpse that ever a herald followed to its urn.
SECOND LORD. His own impatience takes from Aufidius a great part of the blame. Let's make the best of it.

AUFIDIUS. My rage is gone, and I am struck with sorrow. — Take him up. Help, three of the chief soldiers; I'll be one. — Beat the drum, so that it speaks mournfully. — Trail your steel pikes. Though in this city he has widowed and unchilded many a one, who to this hour bewail the injury, yet he shall have a noble memorial. Assist.
[They exit, bearing the body of Martius. A dead march sounds.]
